# Design YouTube

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `YouTube • Google` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The upload of a video is not the video that gets watched: every uploaded file has to be **transcoded** into a whole ladder of resolutions and bitrates before it's watchable, so the real system isn't 'store and serve a file,' it's an ==asynchronous processing pipeline== that sits between the two, and the entire architecture is shaped by keeping that pipeline off the user-facing path.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a video-sharing platform like YouTube: users can upload videos of
arbitrary length and quality, and other users can watch those videos on
a wide range of devices and network conditions, from a phone on 3G to a
4K smart TV on fiber. Design the system end to end, from upload to
playback.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we need to support live streaming, or only pre-recorded, on-demand video?
*Why it matters:* Live video needs a low-latency real-time ingest and transcode path with no room for a slow batch pipeline. Scoping to on-demand only means uploads can be processed asynchronously, which is a fundamentally simpler and more forgiving design.

#### Q: What's the expected video length and file size distribution, and is there an upload size limit?
*Why it matters:* A platform dominated by 30-second clips has very different storage and transcoding economics than one that also accepts multi-hour uploads. This changes chunking strategy, transcoding cost per upload, and storage tiering.

#### Q: Does upload-to-watchable need to be near-instant, or is a delay of a few minutes acceptable?
*Why it matters:* If viewers expect a video to be watchable seconds after upload, the pipeline has to prioritize producing at least one low-resolution rendition fast and backfill higher resolutions later. If a few minutes of delay is fine, the whole ladder can be transcoded before the video goes live, which is much simpler.

#### Q: How important is view count and watch-time accuracy versus just being fast to display?
*Why it matters:* A view counter that must be exact and abuse-resistant needs a very different pipeline (deduplication, bot filtering, delayed reconciliation) than one that just needs to look approximately right in real time, which can be a simple incrementing counter.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can upload a video file, which becomes watchable by others once processing completes.
- A user can watch a video, with the player automatically selecting an appropriate quality for their device and network.
- The system tracks and displays a view count for each video.
- A user can browse a channel page showing all videos uploaded by a given creator.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Playback start latency must be low, ideally under a couple of seconds, regardless of the viewer's location or network quality.**
- **The system must scale storage and delivery for an enormous and ever-growing catalog of large files, without the upload path ever blocking on the full transcoding pipeline.**
- **High availability for playback specifically: a viewer should essentially never see a broken video, even if the upload/processing side is degraded.**
- **The system must tolerate highly uneven load, a small fraction of videos (the ==viral ones==) account for a hugely disproportionate share of total view traffic.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 500 hours of video uploaded per minute globally (a widely cited real-world order of magnitude for a platform this size)
- Average uploaded video is encoded at a source bitrate of about 8 Mbps before transcoding
- Each upload is transcoded into 5 renditions (e.g. 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K where applicable), averaging roughly 1.3x the original file size combined
- 2 billion daily watch sessions, averaging 10 minutes of viewing each

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Raw upload data ingested per day:** 500 hours/min * 60 min/hr * 24 hr = 720,000 hours/day of raw video; at 8 Mbps that's roughly 720,000 * 3,600 * 8 Mbps / 8 bits ≈ 2.6 PB/day of raw uploaded video
- **Total stored data per day, after transcoding:** 2.6 PB raw * 1.3x for the full rendition ladder ≈ 3.4 PB/day added to storage, which is why cheap object storage with lifecycle tiering, not fast local disk, has to be the default
- **Playback bandwidth at peak:** 2 billion sessions/day * 10 min avg, concentrated over peak hours (assume 4 peak hours carry 40% of daily traffic): 800 million sessions * 10 min * 60 sec * ~3 Mbps average delivered bitrate / 8 bits ≈ roughly 1.8 exabytes over those 4 hours, i.e. well over 100 Tbps sustained at peak, which no origin datacenter could serve directly
- **Transcoding compute:** 720,000 hours/day of source video, each hour needing multiple encode passes across 5 renditions; even at a conservative 2x real-time encode speed per rendition, that's 720,000 * 5 / 2 = 1.8 million compute-hours/day, which only a large, elastic, horizontally scaled worker fleet can absorb

*Capacity Takeaway:* The single fact that drives this whole architecture is that **playback bandwidth** (measured in exabytes and 100+ Tbps at peak) is orders of magnitude larger than anything an origin datacenter can serve directly, which is exactly why almost all playback traffic must be pushed out to a CDN, and why the upload/transcode pipeline must be fully decoupled from playback so it never becomes a bottleneck on the read path.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
The upload path and the playback path are almost entirely separate
systems joined only by blob storage and a status field. On upload, the
client gets a pre-signed URL and pushes the raw file straight to blob
storage, bypassing app servers entirely for the large transfer. That
upload event enqueues a transcoding job; a fleet of transcoding workers
pulls jobs off the queue, produces the full rendition ladder, writes each
rendition back to blob storage, and flips the video's status to ready
once enough renditions exist to start serving. On playback, the client
never talks to blob storage or transcoding workers at all: it fetches a
manifest from the app server, then streams video chunks directly from a
CDN edge node that has pulled and cached those renditions from the blob
storage origin. The app servers and database are barely involved in
playback at all, which is deliberate, since playback bandwidth is the
number that dominates this system.

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;

    app["App Servers"]:::server
    blob["Blob Storage (origin)"]:::server

    worker["Transcode Workers"]:::server
    db[("Metadata DB")]:::db
    cdn["CDN Edge"]:::server
    viewer["Viewer"]:::client
    client -->|"request upload URL"| app

    queue -.-> worker
    worker -.->|"write renditions"| blob
    worker -.->|"mark ready"| db

    viewer -->|"stream video chunks"| cdn
```

    step_2["2. Client uploads raw file directly to blob storage (bypasses app servers for the large transfer)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Upload completion enqueues a transcode job (async, off the critical path)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Workers transcode into the rendition ladder (e.g. 240p through 4K, chunked and parallelized)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Renditions written to storage, manifest generated (video status flips to ready)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. CDN pulls and caches renditions on first regional request (subsequent viewers served from the edge)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### A typical video's view rate decay since upload

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/videos` | Initiates an upload: returns a pre-signed URL (or upload session) the client uploads the raw video bytes to directly, bypassing the app server for the large file transfer. |
| `GET` | `/api/videos/{videoId}/status` | Returns processing status (uploading, transcoding, ready, failed) so the client can poll or the UI can show progress before the video is watchable. |
| `GET` | `/api/videos/{videoId}/manifest` | Returns the adaptive streaming manifest (e.g. an HLS/DASH playlist) listing available renditions and their CDN URLs, for the player to select from. |
| `POST` | `/api/videos/{videoId}/view` | Records a view event for the given video, called by the player a few seconds into playback (not on load) to reduce inflated/bot counts. |
| `GET` | `/api/channels/{channelId}/videos` | Returns a paginated list of videos uploaded by a given channel, newest first, for the channel page. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `videos`
- `video_id (unique)`
- `channel_id (indexed)`
- `title, description`
- `status (uploading | transcoding | ready | failed)`
- `duration_seconds`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* The metadata record, small and relational, stored separately from the actual video bytes which live in blob storage keyed by video_id.

### Entity: `renditions`
- `video_id (indexed)`
- `resolution (e.g. 1080p)`
- `bitrate`
- `storage_url (points into blob storage / CDN origin)`
*Notes:* One row per transcoded output of a video. The manifest endpoint assembles its response by reading all ready renditions for a video_id.

### Entity: `view_events`
- `video_id (indexed)`
- `viewer_id_or_session_hash`
- `timestamp`
*Notes:* Written asynchronously via a queue, aggregated into a rolled-up **view_count** on the videos table by a background job rather than incrementing it synchronously on every request, so counting can absorb bot filtering and deduplication without slowing playback.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How should transcoding actually be pipelined, given how much compute it costs?
A single 'transcode the whole video into all resolutions, then mark ready' approach is simple but slow: a 2-hour upload might take many minutes before anything is watchable. A chunk-based approach splits the source video into short segments (e.g. a few seconds each), transcodes segments in parallel across many workers, and can start marking early segments ready before the whole file finishes, letting playback begin before the entire video is done processing.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Whole-file transcoding: simpler to implement and reason about, but upload-to-watchable latency scales with the full video length, which is bad for long uploads
- Chunked, parallel transcoding: much better latency (playback can start once early chunks are ready) and better fault isolation (a failed chunk can be retried without redoing the whole video), but adds real complexity in reassembling chunk boundaries cleanly and keeping chunk-to-manifest bookkeeping consistent
- In practice, large platforms use chunked transcoding specifically because upload volume and video length are both too large for whole-file processing to keep pace

### Where does the video actually get served from: origin storage or CDN?
Blob storage (the origin) is where every rendition is durably stored, but it is not designed to serve massive concurrent read fan-out directly, especially not from users scattered globally. A **CDN** sits in front of it: the first request for a given video segment in a region pulls it from origin and caches it at the edge, every subsequent nearby request is served from that edge cache without touching origin again.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Serving directly from origin storage: simple, always fresh, but origin bandwidth and geographic distance become the bottleneck the moment a video gets popular, and popular videos are exactly the ones with the most viewers furthest from any single datacenter
- CDN in front of origin: dramatically lower latency (edge is physically closer to viewers) and origin load is reduced to roughly one pull per popular segment per edge region, but adds cache-invalidation complexity if a video is ever taken down or re-processed, and cold, unpopular long-tail videos still pay a cache-miss penalty on first request in each region

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Transcoding compute is the biggest elastic-scaling problem on the write side; because it's a large, bursty, parallelizable batch workload, it maps well onto an auto-scaled worker fleet pulling from a queue rather than fixed capacity, so upload spikes don't create a backlog that grows without bound.
- The view-count write path would collapse under synchronous increments at billions of daily views; batching view events through a queue and aggregating asynchronously keeps the hot playback path from ever touching a contended counter.
- Storage cost at this scale demands **tiering**: recently uploaded and popular videos stay on faster, more available storage, while long-tail videos that are rarely watched migrate to cheaper, colder storage classes, since a video's view rate drops sharply within days of upload, and keeping every rendition of every video ever uploaded on the same tier is not economical.
- CDN cache-miss storms for a video going unexpectedly viral in a new region can momentarily hammer origin; a ==request-coalescing== layer at the edge (so many simultaneous misses for the same segment result in one origin fetch, not thousands) prevents that spike from taking down the origin store.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Routing the full video file through an app server== before storing it, instead of letting the client upload directly to blob storage via a pre-signed URL, which needlessly makes the app server a bandwidth bottleneck.
- ⚠️ Treating transcoding as a fast, synchronous step that happens before the API call returns, instead of an asynchronous background pipeline that the client polls or gets notified about.
- ⚠️ Forgetting to mention a CDN at all and assuming the origin storage/datacenter can directly serve global playback traffic, which does not survive the bandwidth math.
- ⚠️ Making view count a synchronous database increment on every playback request, creating write contention on popular videos precisely when the system is under the most load.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't the app servers just serve video bytes directly from blob storage without a CDN?**

> **Model Answer:** Because playback bandwidth at this scale reaches exabytes and well over **100 Tbps at peak**, far more than any single origin's network capacity, and because viewers are geographically distributed while an origin datacenter is not, so every viewer far from the origin would suffer high latency. A CDN solves both problems: it multiplies effective bandwidth by caching at many edge locations and puts content physically closer to viewers.

**Q: Why is transcoding done asynchronously instead of as part of the upload request?**

> **Model Answer:** Transcoding a video into multiple renditions is compute-heavy and can take from seconds to many minutes depending on length, far too slow to hold an HTTP request open for. Decoupling it via a queue and worker fleet lets the upload API return quickly, lets transcoding scale independently and elastically with upload volume, and lets partial failures (one rendition fails) be retried without re-doing the whole upload.

**Q: How would you handle a video that suddenly goes viral minutes after upload, before all renditions and CDN caching have caught up?**

> **Model Answer:** Prioritize producing at least one lower/mid resolution rendition first so the video is watchable quickly, backfill higher resolutions afterward, and rely on CDN request coalescing so a burst of simultaneous viewers in a region results in one origin fetch instead of one per viewer, preventing an origin overload right as the video is becoming popular.

# Design Netflix

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Netflix` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a video-on-demand streaming service like Netflix: a fixed,
professionally produced catalog of movies and shows (not user uploads)
that subscribers stream on demand, with playback that stays smooth even
as their network conditions change mid-stream, and that works well
across a huge range of devices and countries. Design the system end to
end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is content uploaded by users, or is it a curated catalog licensed/produced ahead of time?
*Why it matters:* A fixed, known catalog (thousands to tens of thousands of titles, not millions of uploads a day) changes everything: encoding can be done exhaustively and offline for every title, and content placement at edge nodes can be planned in advance rather than reacted to.

#### Q: Do viewers need the stream to adapt smoothly if their network conditions change mid-playback, like on a mobile network?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether we need true adaptive bitrate streaming (the player switching between pre-encoded quality levels seconds into a stream) versus just picking one bitrate at start time, which is a much simpler but worse experience.

#### Q: Should recommendations and personalization be in scope, or just catalog browsing and playback?
*Why it matters:* Recommendations are a large, separate ML system (built on watch history, collaborative filtering, ranking models) that could consume the entire interview on its own. Scoping it out keeps the focus on the streaming architecture itself.

#### Q: What's the expected concurrency, how many people are streaming simultaneously at peak, like a Friday evening?
*Why it matters:* Concurrent stream count, not catalog size, is what determines total sustained bandwidth needed, and that number is what justifies (or doesn't) building or leasing dedicated edge infrastructure versus using a generic third-party CDN.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A subscriber can browse a catalog of titles and select one to watch.
- A subscriber can start playback, and the stream quality adapts automatically as network conditions change, without the video stopping to buffer unnecessarily.
- A subscriber can resume a title from where they left off, on the same or a different device.
- The system supports multiple profiles per account, each with independent watch history.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Playback must start quickly (sub-2-second startup is the bar) and must not stall or rebuffer noticeably under normal network variation.**
- **The system must sustain enormous simultaneous concurrent streaming load at peak hours (evenings, weekends) without degrading quality for any individual viewer.**
- **The system must serve a global audience with wildly different average network quality and last-mile ISP infrastructure per country/region.**
- **High availability for playback is non-negotiable: a subscriber paying for the service expects it to simply work every time they press play.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 250 million subscribers, of whom roughly 20% are actively streaming during peak evening hours globally staggered by time zone: 50 million concurrent streams at peak
- Average delivered bitrate per stream (blended across devices/resolutions, thanks to adaptive bitrate) is about 3 Mbps
- Catalog size is roughly 15,000 titles, average 1 hour long, each encoded into about 10 bitrate/resolution rungs via modern codecs
- Each hour of source video, once encoded into all 10 rungs, totals roughly 5 GB across the full ladder

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Peak concurrent bandwidth:** 50,000,000 concurrent streams * 3 Mbps ≈ 150 Tbps sustained at peak, which is the number that makes 'serve from a central datacenter' immediately implausible
- **Total encoded catalog size:** 15,000 titles * 1 hour avg * 5 GB/hour (full ladder) = 75 TB for the entire encoded catalog, which is small enough that it's plausible to cache most or all of it at every major edge location
- **Compute cost of encoding a title:** One-time cost per title, not per view: 10 rungs, each taking roughly real-time to a few times real-time to encode well; for a 1-hour title that's a bounded, poolable batch job, utterly different from a live per-upload cost model
- **Edge cache footprint needed to serve most requests locally:** 75 TB total catalog vs. modern edge storage nodes holding tens to low hundreds of TB each, meaning a well-provisioned edge node can hold the entire popular catalog locally, so the vast majority of playback requests never need to reach a distant origin at all

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that shapes this whole design is that 75 TB (the entire encoded catalog) is **small enough to fit at the edge**, while 150 Tbps (peak concurrent playback bandwidth) is ==far too large to serve centrally==, so the winning move is to push nearly the whole catalog out to edge nodes ahead of time rather than fetching it on demand, which is the opposite instinct from a system with a catalog too large to pre-position.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Because the catalog is fixed and known ahead of time, all the expensive
work happens offline, well before playback: every title is encoded once
into a full ladder of resolutions and bitrates, and that entire encoded
catalog (small relative to playback bandwidth) is proactively pushed out
and cached at edge nodes positioned close to or inside ISP networks,
rather than waiting to be pulled on first request. When a subscriber
presses play, the app server returns a manifest of available quality
levels, and the client's adaptive bitrate logic requests video segments
directly from the nearest edge node, continuously measuring throughput
and switching up or down between pre-encoded rungs as conditions change,
entirely on the client side with no server coordination needed
mid-stream. The origin/central systems are involved only for catalog
metadata, licensing checks, and resume-position bookkeeping, never for
the actual video bytes during normal playback.

#### Adaptive bitrate ladder: throughput picks the rung

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts

| `PUT` | `/api/playback/{titleId}/progress` | Body: { position_seconds }. Updates the resume position for the current profile, called periodically during playback and on pause/exit. |
| `GET` | `/api/playback/{titleId}/progress` | Returns the last saved resume position for the current profile, used to offer 'continue watching' on any device. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `titles`
- `title_id (unique)`
- `name, description, genre tags`
- `available_regions (licensing constraints)`
- `duration_seconds`
*Notes:* Small, mostly-read, heavily cached metadata; catalog size is thousands, not billions, of rows, so this table is trivial to keep hot in cache entirely.

### Entity: `renditions`
- `title_id (indexed)`
- `resolution, bitrate, codec`
- `storage_url`
*Notes:* The full bitrate ladder per title, produced once at ingest time, long before any viewer requests it, unlike a user-upload platform where this happens per upload on the critical path.

### Entity: `watch_progress`
- `profile_id (indexed)`
- `title_id`
- `position_seconds`
- `updated_at`

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How does the player pick the right bitrate, and how does it change mid-stream without the video restarting?
The source video is pre-encoded into independent rungs (e.g. 235p at 235 Kbps up through 4K at 16 Mbps), each cut into short segments (a few seconds each) that start and end at the same points across every rung. The client continuously measures its own recent download throughput and buffer health, and for each upcoming segment picks whichever rung best fits current conditions, requesting that segment from whichever rung it chose. Because segment boundaries line up across rungs, switching rungs between segments is seamless, no re-buffering, no restart.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- **Client-driven adaptive bitrate** (what's actually used): the client has the most accurate, lowest-latency view of its own network conditions, and no server round-trip is needed per segment decision, but it means encoding a full ladder for every title up front, which costs storage and one-time encode compute regardless of whether every rung ever gets watched
- Server-driven quality selection: the server could try to pick quality based on coarse signals (device type, region), but it can't react to real-time network fluctuation nearly as well as the client can, leading to worse rebuffering behavior under changing conditions like someone walking from wifi to cellular
- A single fixed bitrate per session (no adaptation): simplest possible design, but breaks down badly the moment network conditions degrade mid-stream, causing stalls instead of a graceful quality drop

### Where should content actually be cached: a generic third-party CDN or purpose-built edge hardware?
A catalog this size (tens of terabytes) can fit almost entirely on edge storage appliances placed directly inside or very close to major ISP networks, an approach sometimes called an open, ISP-embedded edge model. Rather than paying a third-party CDN's transit and delivery costs at massive scale, boxes are shipped to and installed within ISP data centers, pre-loaded with the catalog (or the popular fraction of it) during off-peak hours, so the vast majority of streams never leave the ISP's own network.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Third-party CDN: fast to adopt, no hardware logistics, but at hundreds of Tbps peak scale, delivery costs and shared capacity contention with every other CDN customer become significant, and there's less control over exactly where capacity is placed
- Purpose-built edge boxes embedded in ISP networks: dramatically cheaper at this scale (both to serve, since traffic never leaves the ISP, and for the ISP, since it reduces their own upstream transit costs, making adoption mutually beneficial) and gives full control over pre-positioning content ahead of demand, but requires real hardware logistics, physical installation agreements with ISPs, and forecasting which content to place where
- The realistic answer for a service at this scale is a hybrid: purpose-built edge presence in the ISPs and regions with enough concurrent demand to justify it, generic CDN or central origin fallback for everywhere else, especially newly launched regions

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Peak concurrent bandwidth (150 Tbps in the estimate above), not storage or catalog size, is the dominant constraint; nearly every architectural decision (pre-positioning content, client-driven bitrate adaptation, ISP-embedded edge nodes) exists specifically to keep that number from ever hitting a central origin.
- New or suddenly trending titles create a placement problem: if edge pre-positioning is based on predicted popularity and a title outperforms the prediction, the affected edge nodes can miss more than expected until the next push cycle, so a fallback path to a broader regional cache or origin is needed for under-provisioned titles.
- Watch-progress and profile data, while individually tiny, are accessed at massive scale on every play/pause/seek across hundreds of millions of profiles, and need a fast, globally distributed key-value store rather than a single relational database, so resume-across-devices stays fast everywhere.
- Live events (a real-time exception even for a mostly on-demand system) break the entire pre-encode-and-pre-position model, since there's no time to encode a full ladder or pre-position content in advance, forcing a separate, lower-latency ingest and delivery path for those rare cases.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing the streaming path as if it needs a fan-out or transcoding pipeline on the critical request path==, copying the upload-platform model, when the defining feature of this system is that the catalog is fixed and pre-processed well in advance.
- ⚠️ ==Assuming a generic third-party CDN alone can absorb hundreds of Tbps of peak concurrent load cheaply==, without discussing purpose-built edge placement or the cost/control trade-offs involved.
- ⚠️ Making bitrate selection a server-side decision instead of client-driven, missing why real-time client-side network measurement is what actually makes adaptive streaming responsive to changing conditions.
- ⚠️ Forgetting cross-device resume entirely, or modeling watch-progress as a heavy relational write on every second of playback instead of periodic, lightweight updates.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does Netflix's architecture look so different from a user-generated video platform like YouTube, even though both stream video?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the defining constraint is different: YouTube's catalog is unbounded and arrives continuously as unpredictable uploads, forcing an on-demand, asynchronous transcode pipeline. Netflix's catalog is small, fixed, and known well in advance, so encoding and content placement can both be done exhaustively offline, shifting nearly all the architectural complexity from upload-time processing to playback-time delivery and adaptation.

**Q: Why is adaptive bitrate switching done by the client instead of the server?**

> **Model Answer:** The client has direct, low-latency visibility into its own actual throughput and buffer health, which is exactly the signal needed to choose the right rung for the next segment. A server would only have coarse, indirect signals and a round-trip delay, making it much slower to react to real conditions like a subscriber's wifi degrading mid-episode, so client-driven selection produces far smoother playback.

**Q: What happens if a title becomes unexpectedly popular in a region where it wasn't pre-positioned at the edge?**

> **Model Answer:** Requests for that title's segments miss the local edge cache and fall back to a broader regional cache tier or ultimately the origin, which is slower and more expensive per stream but keeps playback working while the popularity signal propagates and triggers that title to be pushed to the affected edge nodes on the next placement cycle.

Rather than paying a third-party CDN's transit and delivery costs at massive scale, boxes are shipped to and installed within ISP data centers, pre-loaded with the catalog (or the popular fraction of it) during off-peak hours, so the vast majority of streams never leave the ISP's own network.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Third-party CDN: fast to adopt, no hardware logistics, but at hundreds of Tbps peak scale, delivery costs and shared capacity contention with every other CDN customer become significant, and there's less control over exactly where capacity is placed
- Purpose-built edge boxes embedded in ISP networks: dramatically cheaper at this scale (both to serve, since traffic never leaves the ISP, and for the ISP, since it reduces their own upstream transit costs, making adoption mutually beneficial) and gives full control over pre-positioning content ahead of demand, but requires real hardware logistics, physical installation agreements with ISPs, and forecasting which content to place where
- The realistic answer for a service at this scale is a hybrid: purpose-built edge presence in the ISPs and regions with enough concurrent demand to justify it, generic CDN or central origin fallback for everywhere else, especially newly launched regions

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Peak concurrent bandwidth (150 Tbps in the estimate above), not storage or catalog size, is the dominant constraint; nearly every architectural decision (pre-positioning content, client-driven bitrate adaptation, ISP-embedded edge nodes) exists specifically to keep that number from ever hitting a central origin.
- New or suddenly trending titles create a placement problem: if edge pre-positioning is based on predicted popularity and a title outperforms the prediction, the affected edge nodes can miss more than expected until the next push cycle, so a fallback path to a broader regional cache or origin is needed for under-provisioned titles.
- Watch-progress and profile data, while individually tiny, are accessed at massive scale on every play/pause/seek across hundreds of millions of profiles, and need a fast, globally distributed key-value store rather than a single relational database, so resume-across-devices stays fast everywhere.
- Live events (a real-time exception even for a mostly on-demand system) break the entire pre-encode-and-pre-position model, since there's no time to encode a full ladder or pre-position content in advance, forcing a separate, lower-latency ingest and delivery path for those rare cases.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing the streaming path as if it needs a fan-out or transcoding pipeline on the critical request path==, copying the upload-platform model, when the defining feature of this system is that the catalog is fixed and pre-processed well in advance.
- ⚠️ ==Assuming a generic third-party CDN alone can absorb hundreds of Tbps of peak concurrent load cheaply==, without discussing purpose-built edge placement or the cost/control trade-offs involved.
- ⚠️ Making bitrate selection a server-side decision instead of client-driven, missing why real-time client-side network measurement is what actually makes adaptive streaming responsive to changing conditions.
- ⚠️ Forgetting cross-device resume entirely, or modeling watch-progress as a heavy relational write on every second of playback instead of periodic, lightweight updates.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does Netflix's architecture look so different from a user-generated video platform like YouTube, even though both stream video?**

> **Model Answer:** Because the defining constraint is different: YouTube's catalog is unbounded and arrives continuously as unpredictable uploads, forcing an on-demand, asynchronous transcode pipeline. Netflix's catalog is small, fixed, and known well in advance, so encoding and content placement can both be done exhaustively offline, shifting nearly all the architectural complexity from upload-time processing to playback-time delivery and adaptation.

**Q: Why is adaptive bitrate switching done by the client instead of the server?**

> **Model Answer:** The client has direct, low-latency visibility into its own actual throughput and buffer health, which is exactly the signal needed to choose the right rung for the next segment. A server would only have coarse, indirect signals and a round-trip delay, making it much slower to react to real conditions like a subscriber's wifi degrading mid-episode, so client-driven selection produces far smoother playback.

**Q: What happens if a title becomes unexpectedly popular in a region where it wasn't pre-positioned at the edge?**

> **Model Answer:** Requests for that title's segments miss the local edge cache and fall back to a broader regional cache tier or ultimately the origin, which is slower and more expensive per stream but keeps playback working while the popularity signal propagates and triggers that title to be pushed to the affected edge nodes on the next placement cycle.

# Design Spotify

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Spotify` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> An audio file is two orders of magnitude smaller than a video file, which flips the entire caching and delivery economics, so the hard problem here isn't bandwidth, it's keeping a mutable, personal, ordered list (the **playlist**) and a globally trustworthy count (the **royalty-bearing play**) both cheap and correct at hundreds of millions of users.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a music streaming service like Spotify: users can search for songs,
build and edit playlists, stream tracks on demand, and optionally download
tracks for offline listening. Artists and labels need accurate **play counts**
for royalty payments. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How large is the average catalog and how skewed is listening behavior, is it a small set of hits played constantly or a long tail?
*Why it matters:* If a small fraction of tracks account for most plays, nearly the entire hot catalog can live in cache or even on CDN edge nodes permanently, which is a very different design than one where listening is spread evenly across tens of millions of obscure tracks.

#### Q: Does offline download need to work fully offline indefinitely, or just for a bounded period while a subscription is active?
*Why it matters:* Time-limited offline access requires the downloaded file to be tied to a periodically-refreshed license/DRM check, which adds a whole licensing subsystem. Unlimited offline access with no revalidation is simpler but gives up control the business model usually needs.

#### Q: Does a played track need to count toward royalties in real time, or is a batch reconciliation process acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Royalty-bearing play counts need to be ==abuse-resistant== and auditable (a 3-second skip should not count as a play), which pushes toward asynchronous, rule-based aggregation rather than a synchronous counter, similar to but stricter than a vanity view count.

#### Q: Are playlists purely personal, or do we need collaborative playlists that multiple users can edit concurrently?
*Why it matters:* Collaborative editing introduces concurrent-write conflicts on an ordered list (two people reorder or add at once), which needs an explicit conflict-resolution strategy, whereas single-owner playlists are a much simpler ordered-list-per-user problem.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can search for songs, artists, and albums, and start streaming a track within a couple of seconds.
- A user can create, edit, reorder, and delete playlists made up of tracks from the catalog.
- A user can mark tracks or whole playlists for offline download and play them without a network connection.
- The system records each qualifying play so that royalties can be calculated per artist/rights holder.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Playback start latency must be low, on the order of a second or two, even on constrained mobile networks.**
- **The system must scale to a catalog of tens of millions of tracks and hundreds of millions of monthly active users, with read (stream) traffic dwarfing write (upload/catalog-change) traffic.**
- **Play-count data used for royalty payouts must be **accurate and auditable**, favoring correctness over raw speed for that specific pipeline, unlike a vanity metric.**
- **Playlist edits must be immediately visible to the editing user and converge quickly across that user's other devices, even if a brief propagation delay to shared collaborators is acceptable.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 600 million monthly active users, 25% of whom (150 million) stream on a given day
- Average listening session is 60 minutes/day for an active daily user, average track is 3.5 minutes
- Catalog is 100 million tracks, encoded at roughly 128 kbps for standard-quality streaming (audio, unlike video, does not need a full resolution ladder, just a small handful of bitrate tiers)
- Average track file size across quality tiers combined is about 6 MB per track stored

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Tracks streamed per day:** 150,000,000 users * 60 minutes / 3.5 minutes per track ≈ 2.57 billion track-plays/day ≈ 29,700 plays/sec average, far higher at evening peak
- **Peak streaming bandwidth:** At 128 kbps per stream, even a generous 5x peak concentration over 29,700 avg plays/sec ≈ 148,500 concurrent-equivalent streams * 128 kbps / 8 bits ≈ roughly 2.4 GB/sec sustained at peak, three orders of magnitude below a comparable video platform's peak bandwidth
- **Total catalog storage:** 100,000,000 tracks * 6 MB (multiple quality tiers combined) ≈ 600 TB total, small enough that the entire catalog's popular fraction can realistically live at CDN edge or in a large distributed cache
- **Playlist writes per day:** Assume 10% of daily active users edit a playlist an average of 2 times: 15,000,000 * 2 = 30 million playlist edits/day ≈ 350 writes/sec, trivially small next to streaming read volume

*Capacity Takeaway:* Because audio is roughly **50-100x smaller than video** per minute of playback, the entire catalog is small enough (hundreds of TB, not exabytes) that near-total cache/edge coverage of popular tracks is achievable, which means the driving design problem shifts away from raw delivery bandwidth and toward the playlist as a frequently-mutated ordered data structure and the play-count pipeline as an auditable, abuse-resistant ledger.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Search and catalog browsing hit a search index and a metadata database
behind app servers, same shape as any read-heavy catalog service. Playback
is a two-step handoff: the app server authenticates the request and hands
back a short-lived signed URL or manifest, then the client streams audio
bytes directly from a CDN edge node, never touching the app server again
for that stream. Because the catalog is small enough to mostly live at the
edge, cache hit rates are extremely high and origin blob storage is rarely
touched for popular tracks. Playlist edits go through the app server to a
playlists store using an ordered-list representation designed for cheap
inserts and reorders. Every play emits an event onto a queue; workers
aggregate those events, applying royalty-qualifying rules, into a separate
play-count store that is deliberately decoupled from the low-latency
playback path so royalty correctness never adds latency to starting a
song. **Royalty correctness never adds latency to starting a song**.

  e --> f["Rolled into\nplay-count store"]

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/search` | Query params: q, type (track|artist|album). Returns ranked search results from the search index. |
| `GET` | `/api/tracks/{trackId}/stream` | Returns a short-lived signed streaming URL (or manifest) pointing at the appropriate bitrate rendition on the CDN, not the raw file itself. |
| `PATCH` | `/api/playlists/{playlistId}` | Body: { add?: [trackId], remove?: [trackId], reorder?: [trackId, ...] }. Applies an ordered-list edit to a playlist the user owns or collaborates on. |
| `POST` | `/api/tracks/{trackId}/download` | Marks a track for offline download on the requesting device, returns a DRM-wrapped file plus a license that must be periodically revalidated. |
| `POST` | `/api/plays` | Body: { trackId, playedMs }. Called by the client near the end of (or a **threshold** into) a play, feeding the royalty aggregation pipeline rather than incrementing a counter directly. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `tracks`
- `track_id (unique)`
- `artist_id, album_id (indexed)`
- `title, duration_ms`
- `storage_urls (per bitrate rendition, points into blob storage / CDN origin)`
*Notes:* Small metadata rows; actual audio bytes live in blob storage keyed by track_id and bitrate, mirroring the video case study but with far fewer renditions needed.

### Entity: `playlists`
- `playlist_id (unique)`
- `owner_id (indexed)`
- `track_ids (ordered list)`
- `collaborator_ids (nullable)`
- `updated_at`
*Notes:* The ordered list of track_ids is the mutable core of this entity; reordering and inserts need to avoid rewriting the entire list on every edit, typically via **fractional/lexicographic position keys** rather than a plain array index.

### Entity: `play_events`
- `play_event_id`
- `track_id, user_id (indexed)`
- `played_ms, device_id, timestamp`
*Notes:* Raw, immutable log of playback events, written asynchronously via a queue. A separate batch job applies **royalty-qualifying rules** (minimum played duration, dedup per device/session) and aggregates into per-track play counts, kept deliberately separate from any real-time 'now playing' vanity count.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you store and edit a playlist's track order cheaply, especially for very long or frequently-reordered playlists?
The naive representation, an array column of track_ids, means every single reorder or middle-insert rewrites the entire array. A **position-key approach** instead stores each entry with a sortable key (e.g. a fractional number or a string like a base-62 rank) between its neighbors; inserting or moving one track only touches that one row's key, and the list is reconstructed by sorting on the key at read time.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Plain ordered array: simple to read and reason about, but every edit anywhere in a long playlist costs O(n) to rewrite, which gets expensive for playlists with thousands of tracks or frequent reordering
- Fractional/lexicographic position keys: edits become O(1) writes touching only the moved row, but keys can theoretically run out of precision after many edits between the same two neighbors, requiring an occasional rebalancing pass
- In practice, position-key schemes are used specifically because playlist reordering, unlike playlist creation, is a frequent, low-latency-expected operation

### How do you make a royalty-bearing play count trustworthy without slowing down playback?
A naive design increments a play_count column the moment streaming starts, which both creates write contention on hot tracks and is ==trivially gameable== (a 2-second skip counts as a full play, a bot can hammer the endpoint). Instead, the client reports a play event only after a meaningful listening **threshold** (e.g. 30 seconds or half the track), and that event lands on a queue rather than mutating a counter synchronously; a batch aggregation job applies dedup and abuse rules and rolls counts up periodically.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Synchronous counter increment on play start: instantly consistent and simple, but creates hot-row write contention on popular tracks and offers no protection against skips or bot plays, which is unacceptable when real money is paid out per play
- Asynchronous, threshold-gated, batch-aggregated counting: decouples the hot playback path from counting entirely and allows sophisticated abuse/dedup rules, at the cost of the visible play count lagging real listening by minutes to hours
- The royalty pipeline can tolerate that lag because it is a financial ledger, not a live UI number; a separate, looser real-time counter can be shown to users if a live-feeling number is desired for the UI

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Even with a small catalog, a handful of viral tracks can dominate stream volume; edge caching handles this naturally since CDNs are built exactly for hot-object fan-out, unlike the playlist and play-count stores which need their own scaling story.
- The play_events queue and aggregation workers need to keep pace with tens of thousands of events/sec at peak; a backlog here delays royalty accuracy but must never be allowed to block or slow the playback path itself, since the two are deliberately decoupled.
- Very large or highly collaborative playlists (radio-style auto-generated playlists, or playlists with millions of followers making them effectively read-mostly) benefit from being cached aggressively and invalidated only on actual edits, rather than being re-fetched from the primary store on every view.
- Offline license revalidation at scale (checking that a still-subscribed user's cached download remains valid) needs to be a lightweight, infrequent background check per device, not a per-play server round trip, or it would defeat the entire purpose of offline playback.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Modeling a playlist as a plain ordered array of track_ids and not noticing that reordering a 5,000-track playlist becomes an **O(n) rewrite** on every single edit.
- ⚠️ ==Incrementing a play_count column synchronously== the instant a stream starts, which both creates write contention on hit tracks and pays out royalties for plays that were skipped after two seconds.
- ⚠️ Assuming this system needs the same multi-resolution transcoding ladder and CDN bandwidth planning as a video platform, and missing that the much smaller file size fundamentally changes the caching and delivery economics.
- ⚠️ Designing offline download as either a permanent unprotected file or a server call on every offline play, instead of a DRM-licensed file with infrequent background revalidation.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you just increment a play_count column when a user hits play?**

> **Model Answer:** Because that column becomes a **hot-row write contention** point for popular tracks under concurrent load, and more importantly because it has no way to distinguish a genuine listen from a 2-second skip or a bot hammering the endpoint, which matters enormously when real royalty money is paid out per qualifying play. Gating on a listening threshold and aggregating asynchronously through a queue solves both problems at the cost of a lag before the count is fully accurate.

**Q: Why is a fractional/position-key scheme better than a plain array for playlist track order?**

> **Model Answer:** A plain array requires rewriting every entry after the edit point whenever a track is inserted or moved, which is O(n) and gets expensive for long or frequently-reordered playlists. A position-key scheme assigns each track a sortable key placed between its neighbors, so an insert or move only touches the one row being changed, making edits O(1) at the cost of occasionally needing to rebalance keys that have run out of precision between two neighbors.

**Q: Given how much smaller audio files are than video, does this system still need a CDN?**

> **Model Answer:** Yes, latency to the listener still matters even though bandwidth is not the bottleneck it is for video; a CDN puts audio physically close to listeners globally and, because the catalog is small enough to mostly fit at the edge, achieves an even higher cache hit rate than a video platform would, making the CDN cheaper to run per byte served even though it is just as necessary architecturally.

- `track_ids (ordered list)`

*Notes:* The ordered list of track_ids is the mutable core of this entity; reordering and inserts need to avoid rewriting the entire list on every edit, typically via **fractional/lexicographic position keys** rather than a plain array index.

### Entity: `play_events`

*Notes:* Raw, immutable log of playback events, written asynchronously via a queue. A separate batch job applies **royalty-qualifying rules** (minimum played duration, dedup per device/session) and aggregates into per-track play counts, kept deliberately separate from any real-time 'now playing' vanity count.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you store and edit a playlist's track order cheaply, especially for very long or frequently-reordered playlists?
The naive representation, an array column of track_ids, means every single reorder or middle-insert rewrites the entire array. A **position-key approach** instead stores each entry with a sortable key (e.g. a fractional number or a string like a base-62 rank) between its neighbors; inserting or moving one track only touches that one row's key, and the list is reconstructed by sorting on the key at read time.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Plain ordered array: simple to read and reason about, but every edit anywhere in a long playlist costs O(n) to rewrite, which gets expensive for playlists with thousands of tracks or frequent reordering
- Fractional/lexicographic position keys: edits become O(1) writes touching only the moved row, but keys can theoretically run out of precision after many edits between the same two neighbors, requiring an occasional rebalancing pass
- In practice, position-key schemes are used specifically because playlist reordering, unlike playlist creation, is a frequent, low-latency-expected operation

### How do you make a royalty-bearing play count trustworthy without slowing down playback?
A naive design increments a play_count column the moment streaming starts, which both creates write contention on hot tracks and is ==trivially gameable== (a 2-second skip counts as a full play, a bot can hammer the endpoint). Instead, the client reports a play event only after a meaningful listening **threshold** (e.g. 30 seconds or half the track), and that event lands on a queue rather than mutating a counter synchronously; a batch aggregation job applies dedup and abuse rules and rolls counts up periodically.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Synchronous counter increment on play start: instantly consistent and simple, but creates hot-row write contention on popular tracks and offers no protection against skips or bot plays, which is unacceptable when real money is paid out per play
- Asynchronous, threshold-gated, batch-aggregated counting: decouples the hot playback path from counting entirely and allows sophisticated abuse/dedup rules, at the cost of the visible play count lagging real listening by minutes to hours
- The royalty pipeline can tolerate that lag because it is a financial ledger, not a live UI number; a separate, looser real-time counter can be shown to users if a live-feeling number is desired for the UI

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Even with a small catalog, a handful of viral tracks can dominate stream volume; edge caching handles this naturally since CDNs are built exactly for hot-object fan-out, unlike the playlist and play-count stores which need their own scaling story.
- The play_events queue and aggregation workers need to keep pace with tens of thousands of events/sec at peak; a backlog here delays royalty accuracy but must never be allowed to block or slow the playback path itself, since the two are deliberately decoupled.
- Very large or highly collaborative playlists (radio-style auto-generated playlists, or playlists with millions of followers making them effectively read-mostly) benefit from being cached aggressively and invalidated only on actual edits, rather than being re-fetched from the primary store on every view.
- Offline license revalidation at scale (checking that a still-subscribed user's cached download remains valid) needs to be a lightweight, infrequent background check per device, not a per-play server round trip, or it would defeat the entire purpose of offline playback.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Modeling a playlist as a plain ordered array of track_ids and not noticing that reordering a 5,000-track playlist becomes an **O(n) rewrite** on every single edit.
- ⚠️ ==Incrementing a play_count column synchronously== the instant a stream starts, which both creates write contention on hit tracks and pays out royalties for plays that were skipped after two seconds.
- ⚠️ Assuming this system needs the same multi-resolution transcoding ladder and CDN bandwidth planning as a video platform, and missing that the much smaller file size fundamentally changes the caching and delivery economics.
- ⚠️ Designing offline download as either a permanent unprotected file or a server call on every offline play, instead of a DRM-licensed file with infrequent background revalidation.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you just increment a play_count column when a user hits play?**

> **Model Answer:** Because that column becomes a **hot-row write contention** point for popular tracks under concurrent load, and more importantly because it has no way to distinguish a genuine listen from a 2-second skip or a bot hammering the endpoint, which matters enormously when real royalty money is paid out per qualifying play. Gating on a listening threshold and aggregating asynchronously through a queue solves both problems at the cost of a lag before the count is fully accurate.

**Q: Why is a fractional/position-key scheme better than a plain array for playlist track order?**

> **Model Answer:** A plain array requires rewriting every entry after the edit point whenever a track is inserted or moved, which is O(n) and gets expensive for long or frequently-reordered playlists. A position-key scheme assigns each track a sortable key placed between its neighbors, so an insert or move only touches the one row being changed, making edits O(1) at the cost of occasionally needing to rebalance keys that have run out of precision between two neighbors.

**Q: Given how much smaller audio files are than video, does this system still need a CDN?**

> **Model Answer:** Yes, latency to the listener still matters even though bandwidth is not the bottleneck it is for video; a CDN puts audio physically close to listeners globally and, because the catalog is small enough to mostly fit at the edge, achieves an even higher cache hit rate than a video platform would, making the CDN cheaper to run per byte served even though it is just as necessary architecturally.

# Design a Live Streaming Platform (Twitch)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Twitch • YouTube Live` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Every viewer is watching the same seconds of video at the same moment, which means fan-out here is 'one stream to millions of concurrent viewers,' the mirror image of Twitter's 'one post to millions of followers over time,' and the whole system has to trade **latency for scale** on a moving deadline that never gets to relax, because there is no finished file to cache, only the last few seconds that matter.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a live streaming platform like Twitch: a broadcaster pushes a live
video feed from their own encoder, and potentially millions of viewers
watch that same feed simultaneously with only a few seconds of delay,
while also participating in a live text chat alongside the stream. Design
the system end to end, from ingest to viewer playback and chat.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How much end-to-end latency is acceptable between the broadcaster's camera and a viewer's screen?
*Why it matters:* Sub-second latency (for real interactivity) needs a fundamentally different, much more expensive protocol stack (like WebRTC) than 'a few seconds is fine' (which allows chunked HLS/DASH-style delivery through a CDN, dramatically cheaper at scale). This single answer decides almost the entire ingest and delivery architecture.

#### Q: Do all viewers of a given stream need to be in sync with each other (e.g. for shared live reactions), or is a few seconds of per-viewer drift acceptable?
*Why it matters:* CDN edge caching, the only realistic way to serve millions of concurrent viewers, inherently introduces small per-viewer timing differences. Requiring perfect viewer-to-viewer sync would rule out CDN-based delivery entirely and force a much more expensive direct-fan-out architecture.

#### Q: What's the expected distribution of concurrent viewers per stream: mostly small streams, or do a few channels regularly hit hundreds of thousands of simultaneous viewers?
*Why it matters:* A small-streams-only platform could almost get away with simpler direct delivery. A platform with viral, six-figure-concurrent-viewer channels absolutely requires CDN fan-out and multi-bitrate adaptive delivery, since no single origin server can push that much simultaneous bandwidth.

#### Q: Does live chat need message history and moderation tooling, or just best-effort real-time delivery while the stream is live?
*Why it matters:* Chat as a throwaway, high-volume real-time firehose (no durability requirement) is a much simpler pub/sub problem than chat with persistence, replay, and moderation, which starts to need its own storage and indexing layer.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A broadcaster can start a live stream from an encoder (e.g. OBS) and have it become watchable by viewers within a few seconds.
- A viewer can watch any live stream, with the player adapting stream quality to their network conditions.
- Viewers can post and see live chat messages alongside the stream in near real time.
- The stream ends and, optionally, is saved as an on-demand video-on-demand (VOD) replay.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Glass-to-glass latency (camera to viewer screen) should be low, on the order of a few seconds, not tens of seconds, or the product stops feeling live.**
- **The system must support fan-out of a single stream to hundreds of thousands or millions of concurrent viewers without the broadcaster's origin connection being the bottleneck.**
- **High availability for playback: a popular stream going down mid-broadcast affects a huge simultaneous audience at once, so the delivery path needs redundancy the ingest path can tolerate being simpler about.**
- **Chat must handle extremely high message throughput on popular channels (thousands of messages per second) without messages arriving so far out of order or so delayed that the conversation becomes incoherent.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 50,000 concurrent live channels at any given moment, average 200 concurrent viewers per channel, but the top 100 channels average 50,000 concurrent viewers each
- Each stream is ingested at a source bitrate of about 6 Mbps and transcoded into 4 renditions (e.g. source, 1080p, 720p, 480p) for adaptive playback
- Segments are chunked into 2-second pieces for low-latency HLS-style delivery
- Average chat throughput on a large channel during an active moment is roughly 500 messages/sec

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Total concurrent viewers:** (50,000 channels - 100 top channels) * 200 avg + 100 top channels * 50,000 = 49,900 * 200 + 100 * 50,000 ≈ 9.98M + 5M ≈ 15 million concurrent viewers platform-wide
- **Ingest bandwidth:** 50,000 concurrent streams * 6 Mbps ≈ 300 Gbps of raw ingest bandwidth arriving continuously, which must land on a distributed set of ingest points, not one datacenter
- **Transcoding compute:** 50,000 concurrent streams * 4 renditions, each needing real-time (1x) encode speed since this is live, not batch: 200,000 concurrent real-time encode jobs, which must run on a large, elastic, low-latency-optimized worker fleet, very different from YouTube's batch transcoding farm
- **Peak egress bandwidth:** 15,000,000 concurrent viewers * ~3 Mbps average delivered bitrate across the rendition mix / 8 bits ≈ roughly 5.6 Tbps sustained egress, which must be absorbed almost entirely by CDN edge capacity, not origin

*Capacity Takeaway:* The single fact that drives this whole architecture is that a stream has no finished file to fall back on: viewers are all converging on the last few seconds of an ever-growing, never-complete asset, so caching has to work on a **rolling window** of fresh segments (unlike YouTube's cache-forever finished files), and both transcoding and delivery must sustain real-time throughput continuously, with ==zero tolerance for backlog== that on-demand video could absorb.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A broadcaster's encoder pushes video into the nearest geographically
distributed ingest point over a low-latency protocol. From there, a
real-time transcoding fleet (sized and scheduled very differently from a
batch VOD pipeline, since it must sustain continuous 1x-speed encoding per
stream, not just eventually finish) produces a small adaptive-bitrate
rendition ladder, writing short-lived segments that are pushed out through
a CDN built for live, rolling-window content rather than permanent cached
files. Viewers fetch a live manifest that points at the freshest available
segments and their player continuously polls for new ones, giving a few
seconds of glass-to-glass latency. Chat runs as an entirely separate
real-time system: viewers connect over a persistent WebSocket to a pub/sub
fan-out layer that broadcasts each incoming message to every connected
viewer of that channel, decoupled from the video pipeline so a chat spike
never touches video delivery and a video hiccup never drops chat. When the
broadcaster ends the stream, the accumulated segments can optionally be
stitched into a permanent VOD asset and handed off to a conventional
on-demand pipeline.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Live ingest, real-time transcode, CDN fan-out, and a separate chat path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    broadcaster["Broadcaster Encoder"]:::client
    ingest["Ingest Point"]:::server
    transcode["Real-time Transcode Fleet"]:::server
    segstore["Rolling Segment Store"]:::server
    cdn["CDN Edge"]:::server
    viewer["Viewer"]:::client
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    chatpubsub>"Chat Pub/Sub"]:::queue
    broadcaster -->|"RTMP/WebRTC push"| ingest
    ingest -.-> transcode
    transcode -.->|"write rendition segments"| segstore
    segstore -->|"origin pull on miss"| cdn
    viewer -->|"get live manifest"| app
    viewer -->|"stream segments"| cdn
    viewer -.->|"connect + post/receive"| chatpubsub
```

#### Feed fan-out (Twitter) vs live-stream fan-out (Twitch)

| Feed fan-out | Live-stream fan-out |
| :--- | :--- |
| One write, delivered to many stored per-recipient copies over time | One continuously-changing read, delivered to many simultaneous consumers at once |
| Recipients consume asynchronously, whenever they next open the app | Recipients consume synchronously, all watching the same few seconds together |
| Scaling problem is write amplification at post time | Scaling problem is shared-read amplification at CDN edges, in real time |

#### Adaptive bitrate ladder: rendition chosen vs available bandwidth

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST (RTMP/WebRTC ingest, not a typical REST call)` | `/api/streams/{streamKey}/ingest` | The broadcaster's encoder pushes a continuous media stream to the nearest ingest point, authenticated by a per-channel stream key. |
| `GET` | `/api/streams/{channelId}/manifest` | Returns the live adaptive-bitrate manifest (a rolling playlist of the most recent segments across renditions) for the player to begin streaming from. |
| `GET` | `/api/streams/{channelId}/status` | Returns whether a channel is currently live, and basic metadata (title, current viewer count) for the channel page. |
| `WebSocket upgrade` | `/api/chat/{channelId}/connect` | Opens a persistent connection for a viewer to receive live chat messages for a channel and post their own, routed through a pub/sub fan-out layer rather than a request/response API. |
| `POST` | `/api/streams/{channelId}/end` | Called when the broadcaster stops streaming; finalizes the live segments into an optional VOD asset and flips channel status to offline. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `channels`
- `channel_id (unique)`
- `broadcaster_id (indexed)`
- `stream_key (secret, used to authenticate ingest)`
- `status (offline | live)`
- `current_viewer_count (approximate, updated periodically)`
*Notes:* Small, hot metadata row read on nearly every viewer page load; current_viewer_count is deliberately an approximate, periodically-refreshed figure, not a strongly consistent counter, since exactness would require far more coordination than the UI need justifies.

### Entity: `live_segments`
- `channel_id (indexed)`
- `rendition (e.g. 1080p, 720p)`
- `segment_index, segment_url`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* A short, rolling window of the most recent segments per channel per rendition (e.g. last 30-60 seconds), expired and evicted continuously; this is fundamentally different from YouTube's renditions table, which stores a complete, permanent asset.

### Entity: `chat_messages`
- `channel_id (indexed)`
- `user_id, message_text`
- `timestamp`
*Notes:* Optionally persisted for a short retention window (for reconnecting viewers to catch up) or for moderation/replay; the live fan-out path itself is pub/sub and does not wait on this write.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### One stream, millions of viewers: how is this fan-out fundamentally different from a social feed's fan-out problem?
A feed's fan-out problem is 'one post reaches many followers, spread out over however long they each next open the app,' which is why caching a pre-computed per-user timeline works. A live stream's fan-out problem is 'the same few seconds of video must reach every current viewer at nearly the same instant,' which is exactly the shape a CDN's shared edge cache is built for: the first viewer's request in a region pulls a segment from origin, every other simultaneous viewer in that region is served the identical cached segment, so the cost of the 50,001st viewer of the same segment is nearly zero.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Direct server-to-viewer delivery (no CDN): would require origin bandwidth proportional to concurrent viewer count, which is a hard wall around a few thousand viewers per stream at most, nowhere near what a popular channel needs
- CDN edge caching of short rolling segments: scales to millions of concurrent viewers of the same stream at a cost that barely grows past the first viewer per edge region, but requires segments to be short and frequent enough that the caching window stays useful, since live content ages out immediately unlike a permanent VOD file
- This is the inverse of Twitter's fan-out problem: Twitter fans a single write out to many stored copies ahead of time; live streaming fans a single continuously-changing read out to many simultaneous consumers at request time, via shared caching rather than pre-computed per-recipient copies

### Chunked delivery vs a persistent low-latency protocol: how do you choose the ingest-to-viewer pipeline?
Chunked HTTP delivery (segmenting video into small files, e.g. 2-6 seconds each, distributed like any other CDN-cacheable object) is what makes CDN caching possible at all, but each chunk boundary adds latency, typically totaling several seconds end to end. A persistent low-latency protocol like WebRTC can get glass-to-glass latency under a second, but it's a stateful, per-viewer connection that a traditional CDN can't cache or fan out the same way, so it scales far worse for very large simultaneous audiences.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Chunked HTTP (HLS/DASH-style) delivery: scales to millions of concurrent viewers via ordinary CDN caching, at the cost of several seconds of latency from chunking and buffering
- WebRTC-style low-latency delivery: sub-second latency, ideal for truly interactive use cases, but requires per-viewer connections and specialized relay infrastructure (SFUs) that scale far less cheaply than CDN edge caching, making it impractical as the default path for a mass-audience platform
- Most large platforms default to chunked delivery for the mass audience and reserve low-latency protocols for specific interactive use cases (e.g. small co-streaming or watch-party features) where the audience size is naturally bounded

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Ingest points must be geographically distributed close to broadcasters, since a broadcaster on a mediocre home connection uploading to a distant ingest point directly hurts stream quality before the platform even gets involved; this mirrors, in reverse, the CDN-edge-close-to-viewers idea on the delivery side.
- Real-time transcoding capacity has zero slack for backlog, unlike YouTube's batch queue: if the transcoding fleet falls behind even briefly, viewers see stalls or dropped quality in the moment, so this fleet needs aggressive over-provisioning and fast failover, not just eventual elasticity.
- A single viral stream (a major esports final, a celebrity's surprise stream) can spike concurrent viewers on one channel by orders of magnitude in minutes; the CDN and manifest-serving layer need to handle that skew without the rest of the platform's normal-sized streams being starved of capacity.
- Chat fan-out for a top channel at thousands of messages/sec to hundreds of thousands of connected viewers is its own scaling problem, typically solved by a dedicated pub/sub system (sharded by channel) with aggressive server-side rate limiting and client-side message batching, entirely separate from the video scaling story.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing live streaming as if it were on-demand video with a shorter processing delay, missing that the rolling, ever-expiring nature of live segments and the ==zero-tolerance-for-backlog== transcoding requirement are fundamentally different problems.
- ⚠️ Treating chat as just another API endpoint on the same request/response app servers, instead of a dedicated pub/sub fan-out system built for very high message throughput to many simultaneously-connected clients.
- ⚠️ Assuming CDN caching for live content works the same as for on-demand content, without accounting for the short TTL and constant churn of live segments versus permanent cached files.
- ⚠️ ==Reaching for WebRTC as the default delivery mechanism== for the entire mass viewer audience, not realizing it doesn't scale the same way chunked HTTP delivery through a CDN does.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is live-stream fan-out described as the inverse of a social feed's fan-out problem?**

> **Model Answer:** A feed writes one post out to many stored, pre-computed per-follower copies ahead of time, so the scaling cost is concentrated at write/post time. A live stream instead has many viewers simultaneously reading the same continuously-changing content at request time; the scaling cost is concentrated at read time and is absorbed by shared CDN edge caching, where the cost of the Nth simultaneous viewer of the same segment is nearly zero, rather than by pre-computing per-viewer copies.

**Q: Why can't you just use the same batch transcoding architecture as an on-demand video platform for live streams?**

> **Model Answer:** Batch transcoding can queue up and eventually catch up on a backlog without the viewer noticing, since nothing is watchable until it finishes anyway. Live transcoding has no such slack: if the fleet falls behind even briefly, currently-watching viewers see stalls or degraded quality in real time, so the live transcode fleet needs to be sized with continuous real-time throughput and fast failover in mind, not just eventual elastic scaling.

**Q: A single channel suddenly spikes from 500 to 200,000 concurrent viewers during a viral moment. What breaks first, and how do you defend against it?**

> **Model Answer:** The first thing to break is typically CDN origin load if segment caching isn't warmed fast enough for the new demand in each region, followed by chat pub/sub fan-out if message volume also spikes with viewer count. Defenses include request coalescing at CDN edges (many simultaneous cache misses for the same segment collapse into one origin fetch) and having chat fan-out sharded and rate-limited per channel so one viral channel's chat volume doesn't degrade the shared pub/sub infrastructure for other channels.
