broadcaster ends the stream, the accumulated segments can optionally be
stitched into a permanent VOD asset and handed off to a conventional
on-demand pipeline.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Live ingest, real-time transcode, CDN fan-out, and a separate chat path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    broadcaster["Broadcaster Encoder"]:::client
    ingest["Ingest Point"]:::server
    transcode["Real-time Transcode Fleet"]:::server
    segstore["Rolling Segment Store"]:::server
    cdn["CDN Edge"]:::server
    viewer["Viewer"]:::client
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    chatpubsub>"Chat Pub/Sub"]:::queue
    broadcaster -->|"RTMP/WebRTC push"| ingest
    ingest -.-> transcode
    transcode -.->|"write rendition segments"| segstore
    segstore -->|"origin pull on miss"| cdn
    viewer -->|"get live manifest"| app
    viewer -->|"stream segments"| cdn
    viewer -.->|"connect + post/receive"| chatpubsub
```

#### Feed fan-out (Twitter) vs live-stream fan-out (Twitch)

| Feed fan-out | Live-stream fan-out |
| :--- | :--- |
| One write, delivered to many stored per-recipient copies over time | One continuously-changing read, delivered to many simultaneous consumers at once |
| Recipients consume asynchronously, whenever they next open the app | Recipients consume synchronously, all watching the same few seconds together |
| Scaling problem is write amplification at post time | Scaling problem is shared-read amplification at CDN edges, in real time |

#### Adaptive bitrate ladder: rendition chosen vs available bandwidth

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST (RTMP/WebRTC ingest, not a typical REST call)` | `/api/streams/{streamKey}/ingest` | The broadcaster's encoder pushes a continuous media stream to the nearest ingest point, authenticated by a per-channel stream key. |
| `GET` | `/api/streams/{channelId}/manifest` | Returns the live adaptive-bitrate manifest (a rolling playlist of the most recent segments across renditions) for the player to begin streaming from. |
| `GET` | `/api/streams/{channelId}/status` | Returns whether a channel is currently live, and basic metadata (title, current viewer count) for the channel page. |
| `WebSocket upgrade` | `/api/chat/{channelId}/connect` | Opens a persistent connection for a viewer to receive live chat messages for a channel and post their own, routed through a pub/sub fan-out layer rather than a request/response API. |
| `POST` | `/api/streams/{channelId}/end` | Called when the broadcaster stops streaming; finalizes the live segments into an optional VOD asset and flips channel status to offline. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `channels`
- `channel_id (unique)`
- `broadcaster_id (indexed)`
- `stream_key (secret, used to authenticate ingest)`
- `status (offline | live)`
- `current_viewer_count (approximate, updated periodically)`
*Notes:* Small, hot metadata row read on nearly every viewer page load; current_viewer_count is deliberately an approximate, periodically-refreshed figure, not a strongly consistent counter, since exactness would require far more coordination than the UI need justifies.

### Entity: `live_segments`
- `channel_id (indexed)`
- `rendition (e.g. 1080p, 720p)`
- `segment_index, segment_url`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* A short, rolling window of the most recent segments per channel per rendition (e.g. last 30-60 seconds), expired and evicted continuously; this is fundamentally different from YouTube's renditions table, which stores a complete, permanent asset.

### Entity: `chat_messages`
- `channel_id (indexed)`
- `user_id, message_text`
- `timestamp`
*Notes:* Optionally persisted for a short retention window (for reconnecting viewers to catch up) or for moderation/replay; the live fan-out path itself is pub/sub and does not wait on this write.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### One stream, millions of viewers: how is this fan-out fundamentally different from a social feed's fan-out problem?
A feed's fan-out problem is 'one post reaches many followers, spread out over however long they each next open the app,' which is why caching a pre-computed per-user timeline works. A live stream's fan-out problem is 'the same few seconds of video must reach every current viewer at nearly the same instant,' which is exactly the shape a CDN's shared edge cache is built for: the first viewer's request in a region pulls a segment from origin, every other simultaneous viewer in that region is served the identical cached segment, so the cost of the 50,001st viewer of the same segment is nearly zero.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Direct server-to-viewer delivery (no CDN): would require origin bandwidth proportional to concurrent viewer count, which is a hard wall around a few thousand viewers per stream at most, nowhere near what a popular channel needs
- CDN edge caching of short rolling segments: scales to millions of concurrent viewers of the same stream at a cost that barely grows past the first viewer per edge region, but requires segments to be short and frequent enough that the caching window stays useful, since live content ages out immediately unlike a permanent VOD file
- This is the inverse of Twitter's fan-out problem: Twitter fans a single write out to many stored copies ahead of time; live streaming fans a single continuously-changing read out to many simultaneous consumers at request time, via shared caching rather than pre-computed per-recipient copies

### Chunked delivery vs a persistent low-latency protocol: how do you choose the ingest-to-viewer pipeline?
Chunked HTTP delivery (segmenting video into small files, e.g. 2-6 seconds each, distributed like any other CDN-cacheable object) is what makes CDN caching possible at all, but each chunk boundary adds latency, typically totaling several seconds end to end. A persistent low-latency protocol like WebRTC can get glass-to-glass latency under a second, but it's a stateful, per-viewer connection that a traditional CDN can't cache or fan out the same way, so it scales far worse for very large simultaneous audiences.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Chunked HTTP (HLS/DASH-style) delivery: scales to millions of concurrent viewers via ordinary CDN caching, at the cost of several seconds of latency from chunking and buffering
- WebRTC-style low-latency delivery: sub-second latency, ideal for truly interactive use cases, but requires per-viewer connections and specialized relay infrastructure (SFUs) that scale far less cheaply than CDN edge caching, making it impractical as the default path for a mass-audience platform
- Most large platforms default to chunked delivery for the mass audience and reserve low-latency protocols for specific interactive use cases (e.g. small co-streaming or watch-party features) where the audience size is naturally bounded

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Ingest points must be geographically distributed close to broadcasters, since a broadcaster on a mediocre home connection uploading to a distant ingest point directly hurts stream quality before the platform even gets involved; this mirrors, in reverse, the CDN-edge-close-to-viewers idea on the delivery side.
- Real-time transcoding capacity has zero slack for backlog, unlike YouTube's batch queue: if the transcoding fleet falls behind even briefly, viewers see stalls or dropped quality in the moment, so this fleet needs aggressive over-provisioning and fast failover, not just eventual elasticity.
- A single viral stream (a major esports final, a celebrity's surprise stream) can spike concurrent viewers on one channel by orders of magnitude in minutes; the CDN and manifest-serving layer need to handle that skew without the rest of the platform's normal-sized streams being starved of capacity.
- Chat fan-out for a top channel at thousands of messages/sec to hundreds of thousands of connected viewers is its own scaling problem, typically solved by a dedicated pub/sub system (sharded by channel) with aggressive server-side rate limiting and client-side message batching, entirely separate from the video scaling story.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing live streaming as if it were on-demand video with a shorter processing delay, missing that the rolling, ever-expiring nature of live segments and the ==zero-tolerance-for-backlog== transcoding requirement are fundamentally different problems.
- ⚠️ Treating chat as just another API endpoint on the same request/response app servers, instead of a dedicated pub/sub fan-out system built for very high message throughput to many simultaneously-connected clients.
- ⚠️ Assuming CDN caching for live content works the same as for on-demand content, without accounting for the short TTL and constant churn of live segments versus permanent cached files.
- ⚠️ ==Reaching for WebRTC as the default delivery mechanism== for the entire mass viewer audience, not realizing it doesn't scale the same way chunked HTTP delivery through a CDN does.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is live-stream fan-out described as the inverse of a social feed's fan-out problem?**

> **Model Answer:** A feed writes one post out to many stored, pre-computed per-follower copies ahead of time, so the scaling cost is concentrated at write/post time. A live stream instead has many viewers simultaneously reading the same continuously-changing content at request time; the scaling cost is concentrated at read time and is absorbed by shared CDN edge caching, where the cost of the Nth simultaneous viewer of the same segment is nearly zero, rather than by pre-computing per-viewer copies.

**Q: Why can't you just use the same batch transcoding architecture as an on-demand video platform for live streams?**

> **Model Answer:** Batch transcoding can queue up and eventually catch up on a backlog without the viewer noticing, since nothing is watchable until it finishes anyway. Live transcoding has no such slack: if the fleet falls behind even briefly, currently-watching viewers see stalls or degraded quality in real time, so the live transcode fleet needs to be sized with continuous real-time throughput and fast failover in mind, not just eventual elastic scaling.

**Q: A single channel suddenly spikes from 500 to 200,000 concurrent viewers during a viral moment. What breaks first, and how do you defend against it?**

> **Model Answer:** The first thing to break is typically CDN origin load if segment caching isn't warmed fast enough for the new demand in each region, followed by chat pub/sub fan-out if message volume also spikes with viewer count. Defenses include request coalescing at CDN edges (many simultaneous cache misses for the same segment collapse into one origin fetch) and having chat fan-out sharded and rate-limited per channel so one viral channel's chat volume doesn't degrade the shared pub/sub infrastructure for other channels.

# Design a Podcast Platform

> **Difficulty:** `EASY` | **Target Companies:** `Apple Podcasts • Spotify` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A podcast episode is a **static file** published once and distributed the same way to everyone, closer to a blog post with an attached audio file than a proprietary streaming pipeline, so the genuinely hard part of this system isn't delivery at all, it's keeping one listener's **playback position** consistent and quickly available across every device they own.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a podcast platform like Apple Podcasts: creators publish episodes
under a show, and listeners subscribe to shows, then stream or download
episodes and have their **playback position** remembered and synced across
their devices. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we own the distribution end to end, or does the platform need to support the open **RSS-feed model** where any podcast app can pull episodes from any show's feed?
*Why it matters:* The open RSS model means episode files just need to be publicly fetchable static files at stable URLs, with no proprietary streaming protocol or ==DRM== required at all, which massively simplifies delivery compared to a closed platform. It also means the platform must be a well-behaved RSS producer and, if it aggregates other shows, an RSS consumer too.

#### Q: How important is exact **playback-position sync** across a listener's devices, versus best-effort?
*Why it matters:* If a listener stops on their phone mid-commute and expects to resume at the exact second on their laptop, that needs a low-latency, frequently-updated sync mechanism. If a few seconds or minutes of drift is acceptable, a much simpler ==periodic sync== suffices, which changes how chatty the client-server position updates need to be.

#### Q: Should listeners be able to download episodes for offline playback, and if so, does that need any content protection?
*Why it matters:* Podcasts are typically not DRM-protected content (unlike a paid music catalog), so offline download is usually just 'fetch the file and store it locally,' with no licensing/revalidation system needed, a much simpler offline story than a subscription music or video service.

#### Q: Do episodes need transcoding into multiple bitrates/formats, or is a single fixed-quality audio file sufficient?
*Why it matters:* Most podcast platforms serve the **single file** the creator uploaded (maybe normalized to one standard bitrate), rather than building a full adaptive-bitrate rendition ladder, since spoken-word audio tolerates a single moderate bitrate far better than music or video tolerates a single quality tier. This avoids an entire transcoding pipeline that on-demand video or high-fidelity music streaming can't avoid.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A creator can publish a show and add episodes to it, each with audio, title, description, and publish date.
- A listener can subscribe to a show and see new episodes appear automatically, similar to following an RSS feed.
- A listener can stream or download an episode and play it back, with the player showing accurate duration and allowing seeking.
- A listener's **playback position** within an episode is saved and available across their other devices.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Episode publishing (from creator upload to listener-visible) should complete within minutes, not require the multi-stage low-latency pipeline a live platform needs.**
- **The system must scale to millions of shows and a ==long tail== of episodes, most of which are rarely played, so storage cost per rarely-accessed episode matters more than peak delivery bandwidth.**
- ****Playback-position sync** should feel near-instant when switching devices for an actively-used account, without requiring a constant open connection between devices.**
- **The system should remain interoperable with the broader RSS-based podcast ecosystem, so shows aren't locked into a single proprietary app.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million active shows, averaging 2 new episodes per week per active show, each episode averaging 40 minutes at a modest 64 kbps (spoken-word doesn't need music-grade bitrate)
- 80 million monthly active listeners, each averaging 3 hours of listening per week
- Listening is heavily long-tail: a small fraction of shows account for a large share of plays, but even niche shows need to remain available indefinitely
- Playback position is saved roughly every 15-30 seconds during active playback

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **New episode storage added per week:** 5,000,000 shows * 2 episodes * 40 min * 60 sec * 64 kbps / 8 bits ≈ 5,000,000 * 2 * 2,400 sec * 8 KB/sec ≈ roughly 192 TB added per week, modest next to a video platform's daily ingest
- **Peak streaming bandwidth:** 80,000,000 listeners * 3 hrs/week, concentrated in commute-hour peaks (assume 4 peak hours/day carry 25% of weekly listening): roughly 60 million listener-hours/week * 0.25 / (4 hrs * 7 days) ≈ 535,000 concurrent-equivalent listeners at peak * 64 kbps / 8 bits ≈ roughly 4.3 GB/sec at peak, small enough that a CDN handles it comfortably without exotic scaling
- **Playback-position writes:** Assume 10 million concurrent daily listening sessions at any given moment during peak, each posting a position update every 20 sec on average: 10,000,000 / 20 = **500,000 position writes/sec** at absolute peak, which is the actual hot path this system needs to be built around, not audio delivery

*Capacity Takeaway:* Audio delivery bandwidth here is small enough (a few GB/sec at peak) to be a solved problem via ordinary CDN caching of static files, so the single fact that actually shapes this design is that **playback-position updates**, a small, frequent, per-listener write, vastly outnumber episode publishes and need their own lightweight, high-throughput, eventually-consistent sync path rather than living in the same store as show and episode metadata.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Publishing is the simple path: a creator uploads an episode's audio file
directly to blob storage via a pre-signed URL, the episode's metadata is
written to the catalog database, and the show's RSS feed is regenerated
(or generated on the fly from the catalog) to include the new episode.
Listening mirrors any static-file delivery system: the app server returns
episode metadata and an audio URL, and the actual bytes are served from a
CDN in front of blob storage, since podcast audio needs no proprietary
streaming protocol or per-request transcoding decision, just a normal
cacheable file. The one path that is genuinely different from a typical
catalog-plus-CDN system is playback-position sync: as a listener plays an
episode, their client periodically writes their current position to a
small, fast, separate key-value store keyed by listener and episode, and
every device the listener owns reads from that same store when opening an
episode, so resuming on a new device just means fetching the **latest
written position** rather than any real-time push between devices.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Publish path, static-file delivery, and the separate position-sync path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    creator["Creator"]:::client
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    blob["Blob Storage (origin)"]:::server
    catalogdb[("Catalog DB (shows/episodes)")]:::db
    cdn["CDN Edge"]:::server
    listener["Listener"]:::client
    posdb["Position Store"]:::cache
    creator -->|"upload episode"| app
    app -->|"store audio file"| blob
    app -->|"write episode metadata"| catalogdb
    listener -->|"get episode / RSS feed"| app
    listener -->|"stream/download audio"| cdn
    blob -->|"origin pull on miss"| cdn
    listener -.->|"read/write playback position"| posdb
```

#### Streaming vs downloading an episode

| Streaming | Downloading |
| :--- | :--- |
| No local storage used, always plays the latest published version | Uses device storage, but plays anywhere with no connection |
| Needs a network connection at play time | Ideal for mobile listeners with unreliable or costly data (commutes, flights) |
| Simple, works well on stable connections | No DRM needed, unlike a paid music/video service, since the file is just copied locally |

#### Cross-device resume: periodic write, read-latest-on-open

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Phone
  participant PosStore as Position Store
  participant Laptop
  Phone->>PosStore: write position (every 15-30s)
  Phone->>PosStore: write position (on pause)
  Laptop->>PosStore: open episode, read latest
  PosStore-->>Laptop: last written position
  Laptop->>Laptop: resume playback there
```

#### Long-tail play distribution across shows

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/shows/{showId}/episodes` | Creator publishes a new episode: body includes an audio file reference (via a pre-signed upload URL, similar to other media platforms), title, description, publish_at. |
| `GET` | `/feeds/{showId}/rss.xml` | Public, unauthenticated RSS feed for a show, the same feed any third-party podcast app can subscribe to; this is the platform's standard distribution format, not a proprietary API. |
| `POST` | `/api/subscriptions` | Body: { showId }. Subscribes the authenticated listener to a show so new episodes surface in their library. |
| `PUT` | `/api/episodes/{episodeId}/position` | Body: { positionSeconds, deviceId, updatedAt }. **Upserts** the listener's current playback position for an episode, called periodically during playback. |
| `GET` | `/api/episodes/{episodeId}/position` | Returns the listener's most recent playback position for an episode across all their devices, used when resuming playback on any device. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `shows`
- `show_id (unique)`
- `creator_id (indexed)`
- `title, description, rss_feed_url`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* The show is the RSS-feed-equivalent unit; each show's episodes render into a standard RSS XML document served at a stable public URL.

### Entity: `episodes`
- `episode_id (unique)`
- `show_id (indexed)`
- `title, description, duration_seconds`
- `audio_url (points into blob storage / CDN origin)`
- `published_at`
*Notes:* Unlike a video platform, there is typically just one stored audio rendition per episode rather than a multi-bitrate ladder, since spoken-word tolerates a single moderate bitrate well.

### Entity: `playback_positions`
- `listener_id, episode_id (composite key, indexed)`
- `position_seconds`
- `device_id, updated_at`
*Notes:* Deliberately a small, separate, **high-write-throughput** store (a distributed key-value store or cache-backed table), not colocated with show/episode metadata, since its access pattern (frequent small upserts keyed by listener+episode) is completely different from the read-heavy, rarely-written catalog data.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you sync playback position across devices without an always-open connection between them?
Devices aren't directly connected to each other; they're each connected to the server independently and at different times. The client periodically (e.g. every 15-30 seconds during playback, and on pause/stop) writes its current position, tagged with a timestamp and device ID, to a shared position store. Any device, on opening that episode, simply reads the **latest position** by timestamp for that listener. There's no push notification needed between devices, the ==read-latest-write model== is sufficient because a listener only actively uses one device at a time in the overwhelming majority of cases.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- **Push-based real-time sync** (server notifies other devices immediately on a position update): near-instant cross-device consistency, but requires maintaining open connections (WebSocket/push) per listener across all their devices for a benefit that matters only in the rare case they switch devices mid-episode within seconds
- Periodic write, read-latest-on-open model: no persistent connections needed, trivially scales as a simple key-value read/write, and the small staleness window (at most one update interval) is invisible in practice since a listener switching devices mid-playback almost always pauses first, which itself triggers an immediate write
- The read-latest model is the practical choice because the cost of the rare edge case (extremely fast device switch losing a few seconds of position) is far lower than the cost of maintaining always-on connections for every listening session

### Should the position store share a database with show/episode metadata, or be a separate system?
Show and episode metadata is **read-heavy**, written rarely (a new episode every few days per show at most), and benefits from being colocated with search/browse features. Playback positions are the opposite: **write-heavy** (every 15-30 seconds per active listening session), read only on episode open, and don't need any of the relational structure or indexing that catalog browsing needs.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- One shared database for both: simpler operationally (one system to run), but the position table's high write frequency risks contending with or degrading the catalog database that search and browse features depend on
- A separate key-value store (or cache-backed store) just for positions: isolates the high-frequency write load from catalog reads entirely, and can be tuned/scaled independently (e.g. accept eventual consistency, use TTL-based cleanup for abandoned episodes), at the cost of one more system to operate and keep available
- Given that position writes were estimated to be the actual peak-throughput hot path of this whole system, isolating them is the right default, mirroring how other case studies separate a hot, high-frequency write path (like view counts) from the main catalog store

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Playback-position writes are the highest-throughput operation in the system by a wide margin, so that store needs to be a lightweight, **horizontally-shardable** key-value store (sharded by listener_id or episode_id) rather than a relational table with heavier write overhead.
- RSS feed generation for very large shows (or an aggregator serving many shows) should be cached and only regenerated on actual new-episode publishes, not rebuilt from scratch on every feed fetch, since third-party podcast apps poll feeds frequently and predictably.
- ==Long-tail episodes== (the vast majority, rarely played) should move to cheaper, colder storage tiers over time, similar to any large media catalog, since keeping every episode ever published on hot storage doesn't match the actual access pattern.
- A single viral episode can spike download/stream requests briefly, but because files are static and CDN-cacheable (unlike live content), this is the easiest kind of spike for the system to absorb, ordinary cache warm-up handles it without special-casing.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing a full multi-bitrate transcoding pipeline== like a video platform's, when most podcast audio only needs a single normalized-bitrate file, adding unnecessary pipeline complexity.
- ⚠️ Treating playback-position sync as an afterthought detail instead of recognizing it as the **highest-frequency write path** in the entire system, and colocating it with the catalog database where it can contend with browse/search reads.
- ⚠️ Forgetting the RSS-feed distribution model entirely and designing the platform as a fully closed system, missing a core functional expectation of how podcasts actually get distributed and discovered.
- ⚠️ Over-engineering cross-device sync with real-time push/WebSocket connections per listener when a simple periodic-write, read-latest model solves the actual use case with far less infrastructure.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't this platform need the same adaptive-bitrate transcoding ladder that a video or music-streaming platform needs?**

> **Model Answer:** Spoken-word podcast audio tolerates a single, moderate, normalized bitrate (e.g. 64-96 kbps) well, unlike video where visual quality differences are obvious and network conditions vary widely enough to need multiple tiers. Most platforms store one file per episode rather than a rendition ladder, trading a small amount of flexibility on poor networks for a dramatically simpler pipeline with no transcoding fleet needed at all.

**Q: Why is playback-position sync described as the actual hot path of this system, rather than audio streaming?**

> **Model Answer:** Audio delivery is infrequent per listener (starting an episode) and cheaply served as a static cached file through a CDN. Position updates happen continuously throughout every active listening session, every 15-30 seconds, across tens of millions of concurrent sessions at peak, which the capacity estimate shows produces far more **write operations per second** than episode publishes or even episode-open events, making it the part of the system that most needs its own scalable, isolated design.

**Q: How would you keep the RSS feed for a large show from becoming a bottleneck, given third-party apps poll it frequently?**

> **Model Answer:** Cache the generated feed XML and only regenerate it when a new episode is actually published, rather than rebuilding it from the catalog database on every fetch, since polling volume from external apps checking for new episodes is predictable and far higher than the rate of actual publishes. Serving the cached feed through a CDN like any other cacheable static resource further reduces load on the app servers and catalog database.

*Why it matters:* Podcasts are typically not DRM-protected content (unlike a paid music catalog), so offline download is usually just 'fetch the file and store it locally,' with no licensing/revalidation system needed, a much simpler offline story than a subscription music or video service.

#### Q: Do episodes need transcoding into multiple bitrates/formats, or is a single fixed-quality audio file sufficient?
*Why it matters:* Most podcast platforms serve the **single file** the creator uploaded (maybe normalized to one standard bitrate), rather than building a full adaptive-bitrate rendition ladder, since spoken-word audio tolerates a single moderate bitrate far better than music or video tolerates a single quality tier. This avoids an entire transcoding pipeline that on-demand video or high-fidelity music streaming can't avoid.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A creator can publish a show and add episodes to it, each with audio, title, description, and publish date.
- A listener can subscribe to a show and see new episodes appear automatically, similar to following an RSS feed.
- A listener can stream or download an episode and play it back, with the player showing accurate duration and allowing seeking.
- A listener's **playback position** within an episode is saved and available across their other devices.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Episode publishing (from creator upload to listener-visible) should complete within minutes, not require the multi-stage low-latency pipeline a live platform needs.**
- **The system must scale to millions of shows and a ==long tail== of episodes, most of which are rarely played, so storage cost per rarely-accessed episode matters more than peak delivery bandwidth.**
- ****Playback-position sync** should feel near-instant when switching devices for an actively-used account, without requiring a constant open connection between devices.**
- **The system should remain interoperable with the broader RSS-based podcast ecosystem, so shows aren't locked into a single proprietary app.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million active shows, averaging 2 new episodes per week per active show, each episode averaging 40 minutes at a modest 64 kbps (spoken-word doesn't need music-grade bitrate)
- 80 million monthly active listeners, each averaging 3 hours of listening per week
- Listening is heavily long-tail: a small fraction of shows account for a large share of plays, but even niche shows need to remain available indefinitely
- Playback position is saved roughly every 15-30 seconds during active playback

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **New episode storage added per week:** 5,000,000 shows * 2 episodes * 40 min * 60 sec * 64 kbps / 8 bits ≈ 5,000,000 * 2 * 2,400 sec * 8 KB/sec ≈ roughly 192 TB added per week, modest next to a video platform's daily ingest
- **Peak streaming bandwidth:** 80,000,000 listeners * 3 hrs/week, concentrated in commute-hour peaks (assume 4 peak hours/day carry 25% of weekly listening): roughly 60 million listener-hours/week * 0.25 / (4 hrs * 7 days) ≈ 535,000 concurrent-equivalent listeners at peak * 64 kbps / 8 bits ≈ roughly 4.3 GB/sec at peak, small enough that a CDN handles it comfortably without exotic scaling
- **Playback-position writes:** Assume 10 million concurrent daily listening sessions at any given moment during peak, each posting a position update every 20 sec on average: 10,000,000 / 20 = **500,000 position writes/sec** at absolute peak, which is the actual hot path this system needs to be built around, not audio delivery

*Capacity Takeaway:* Audio delivery bandwidth here is small enough (a few GB/sec at peak) to be a solved problem via ordinary CDN caching of static files, so the single fact that actually shapes this design is that **playback-position updates**, a small, frequent, per-listener write, vastly outnumber episode publishes and need their own lightweight, high-throughput, eventually-consistent sync path rather than living in the same store as show and episode metadata.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Publishing is the simple path: a creator uploads an episode's audio file
directly to blob storage via a pre-signed URL, the episode's metadata is
written to the catalog database, and the show's RSS feed is regenerated
(or generated on the fly from the catalog) to include the new episode.
Listening mirrors any static-file delivery system: the app server returns
episode metadata and an audio URL, and the actual bytes are served from a
CDN in front of blob storage, since podcast audio needs no proprietary
streaming protocol or per-request transcoding decision, just a normal
cacheable file. The one path that is genuinely different from a typical
catalog-plus-CDN system is playback-position sync: as a listener plays an
episode, their client periodically writes their current position to a
small, fast, separate key-value store keyed by listener and episode, and
every device the listener owns reads from that same store when opening an
episode, so resuming on a new device just means fetching the **latest
written position** rather than any real-time push between devices.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Publish path, static-file delivery, and the separate position-sync path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    creator["Creator"]:::client
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    blob["Blob Storage (origin)"]:::server
    catalogdb[("Catalog DB (shows/episodes)")]:::db
    cdn["CDN Edge"]:::server
    listener["Listener"]:::client
    posdb["Position Store"]:::cache
    creator -->|"upload episode"| app
    app -->|"store audio file"| blob
    app -->|"write episode metadata"| catalogdb
    listener -->|"get episode / RSS feed"| app
    listener -->|"stream/download audio"| cdn
    blob -->|"origin pull on miss"| cdn
    listener -.->|"read/write playback position"| posdb
```

#### Streaming vs downloading an episode

| Streaming | Downloading |
| :--- | :--- |
| No local storage used, always plays the latest published version | Uses device storage, but plays anywhere with no connection |
| Needs a network connection at play time | Ideal for mobile listeners with unreliable or costly data (commutes, flights) |
| Simple, works well on stable connections | No DRM needed, unlike a paid music/video service, since the file is just copied locally |

#### Cross-device resume: periodic write, read-latest-on-open

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Phone
  participant PosStore as Position Store
  participant Laptop
  Phone->>PosStore: write position (every 15-30s)
  Phone->>PosStore: write position (on pause)
  Laptop->>PosStore: open episode, read latest
  PosStore-->>Laptop: last written position
  Laptop->>Laptop: resume playback there
```

#### Long-tail play distribution across shows

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/shows/{showId}/episodes` | Creator publishes a new episode: body includes an audio file reference (via a pre-signed upload URL, similar to other media platforms), title, description, publish_at. |
| `GET` | `/feeds/{showId}/rss.xml` | Public, unauthenticated RSS feed for a show, the same feed any third-party podcast app can subscribe to; this is the platform's standard distribution format, not a proprietary API. |
| `POST` | `/api/subscriptions` | Body: { showId }. Subscribes the authenticated listener to a show so new episodes surface in their library. |
| `PUT` | `/api/episodes/{episodeId}/position` | Body: { positionSeconds, deviceId, updatedAt }. **Upserts** the listener's current playback position for an episode, called periodically during playback. |
| `GET` | `/api/episodes/{episodeId}/position` | Returns the listener's most recent playback position for an episode across all their devices, used when resuming playback on any device. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `shows`
- `show_id (unique)`
- `creator_id (indexed)`
- `title, description, rss_feed_url`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* The show is the RSS-feed-equivalent unit; each show's episodes render into a standard RSS XML document served at a stable public URL.

### Entity: `episodes`
- `episode_id (unique)`
- `show_id (indexed)`
- `title, description, duration_seconds`
- `audio_url (points into blob storage / CDN origin)`
- `published_at`
*Notes:* Unlike a video platform, there is typically just one stored audio rendition per episode rather than a multi-bitrate ladder, since spoken-word tolerates a single moderate bitrate well.

### Entity: `playback_positions`
- `listener_id, episode_id (composite key, indexed)`
- `position_seconds`
- `device_id, updated_at`
*Notes:* Deliberately a small, separate, **high-write-throughput** store (a distributed key-value store or cache-backed table), not colocated with show/episode metadata, since its access pattern (frequent small upserts keyed by listener+episode) is completely different from the read-heavy, rarely-written catalog data.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you sync playback position across devices without an always-open connection between them?
Devices aren't directly connected to each other; they're each connected to the server independently and at different times. The client periodically (e.g. every 15-30 seconds during playback, and on pause/stop) writes its current position, tagged with a timestamp and device ID, to a shared position store. Any device, on opening that episode, simply reads the **latest position** by timestamp for that listener. There's no push notification needed between devices, the ==read-latest-write model== is sufficient because a listener only actively uses one device at a time in the overwhelming majority of cases.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- **Push-based real-time sync** (server notifies other devices immediately on a position update): near-instant cross-device consistency, but requires maintaining open connections (WebSocket/push) per listener across all their devices for a benefit that matters only in the rare case they switch devices mid-episode within seconds
- Periodic write, read-latest-on-open model: no persistent connections needed, trivially scales as a simple key-value read/write, and the small staleness window (at most one update interval) is invisible in practice since a listener switching devices mid-playback almost always pauses first, which itself triggers an immediate write
- The read-latest model is the practical choice because the cost of the rare edge case (extremely fast device switch losing a few seconds of position) is far lower than the cost of maintaining always-on connections for every listening session

### Should the position store share a database with show/episode metadata, or be a separate system?
Show and episode metadata is **read-heavy**, written rarely (a new episode every few days per show at most), and benefits from being colocated with search/browse features. Playback positions are the opposite: **write-heavy** (every 15-30 seconds per active listening session), read only on episode open, and don't need any of the relational structure or indexing that catalog browsing needs.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- One shared database for both: simpler operationally (one system to run), but the position table's high write frequency risks contending with or degrading the catalog database that search and browse features depend on
- A separate key-value store (or cache-backed store) just for positions: isolates the high-frequency write load from catalog reads entirely, and can be tuned/scaled independently (e.g. accept eventual consistency, use TTL-based cleanup for abandoned episodes), at the cost of one more system to operate and keep available
- Given that position writes were estimated to be the actual peak-throughput hot path of this whole system, isolating them is the right default, mirroring how other case studies separate a hot, high-frequency write path (like view counts) from the main catalog store

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Playback-position writes are the highest-throughput operation in the system by a wide margin, so that store needs to be a lightweight, **horizontally-shardable** key-value store (sharded by listener_id or episode_id) rather than a relational table with heavier write overhead.
- RSS feed generation for very large shows (or an aggregator serving many shows) should be cached and only regenerated on actual new-episode publishes, not rebuilt from scratch on every feed fetch, since third-party podcast apps poll feeds frequently and predictably.
- ==Long-tail episodes== (the vast majority, rarely played) should move to cheaper, colder storage tiers over time, similar to any large media catalog, since keeping every episode ever published on hot storage doesn't match the actual access pattern.
- A single viral episode can spike download/stream requests briefly, but because files are static and CDN-cacheable (unlike live content), this is the easiest kind of spike for the system to absorb, ordinary cache warm-up handles it without special-casing.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Designing a full multi-bitrate transcoding pipeline== like a video platform's, when most podcast audio only needs a single normalized-bitrate file, adding unnecessary pipeline complexity.
- ⚠️ Treating playback-position sync as an afterthought detail instead of recognizing it as the **highest-frequency write path** in the entire system, and colocating it with the catalog database where it can contend with browse/search reads.
- ⚠️ Forgetting the RSS-feed distribution model entirely and designing the platform as a fully closed system, missing a core functional expectation of how podcasts actually get distributed and discovered.
- ⚠️ Over-engineering cross-device sync with real-time push/WebSocket connections per listener when a simple periodic-write, read-latest model solves the actual use case with far less infrastructure.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why doesn't this platform need the same adaptive-bitrate transcoding ladder that a video or music-streaming platform needs?**

> **Model Answer:** Spoken-word podcast audio tolerates a single, moderate, normalized bitrate (e.g. 64-96 kbps) well, unlike video where visual quality differences are obvious and network conditions vary widely enough to need multiple tiers. Most platforms store one file per episode rather than a rendition ladder, trading a small amount of flexibility on poor networks for a dramatically simpler pipeline with no transcoding fleet needed at all.

**Q: Why is playback-position sync described as the actual hot path of this system, rather than audio streaming?**

> **Model Answer:** Audio delivery is infrequent per listener (starting an episode) and cheaply served as a static cached file through a CDN. Position updates happen continuously throughout every active listening session, every 15-30 seconds, across tens of millions of concurrent sessions at peak, which the capacity estimate shows produces far more **write operations per second** than episode publishes or even episode-open events, making it the part of the system that most needs its own scalable, isolated design.

**Q: How would you keep the RSS feed for a large show from becoming a bottleneck, given third-party apps poll it frequently?**

> **Model Answer:** Cache the generated feed XML and only regenerate it when a new episode is actually published, rather than rebuilding it from the catalog database on every fetch, since polling volume from external apps checking for new episodes is predictable and far higher than the rate of actual publishes. Serving the cached feed through a CDN like any other cacheable static resource further reduces load on the app servers and catalog database.

# Design an Image Hosting Service (like Flickr)

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Flickr • Imgur` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> An image is immutable binary data with structured metadata bolted on, so the entire design comes down to separating those two concerns cleanly: a **blob store** built for cheap, massive, mostly-write-once binary storage, and a small database that only tracks where each blob lives and what it's called.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design an image hosting service: a user uploads an image, the system stores
it and generates a few common resolutions (thumbnail, medium, full-size),
and anyone with the link can view the image quickly from anywhere in the
world. Design the system end to end. You don't need to design a full social
network around it, just the upload, storage, resizing, and serving.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the read-to-write ratio, and how much does traffic concentrate on a small number of popular images?
*Why it matters:* Image hosting is typically extremely read-heavy, and popularity is skewed (a handful of images get most of the views). That skew is what justifies putting a CDN in front of nearly everything rather than serving directly from storage.

#### Q: Do we need to generate multiple resolutions (thumbnail, medium, full-size), or serve the exact bytes that were uploaded?
*Why it matters:* Multi-resolution support means an asynchronous processing pipeline has to exist between upload and 'the image is fully available', which changes both the write path and the data model (one logical image, several physical variants).

#### Q: What's the maximum image size and expected upload volume, and do we need to support very large original files (e.g. RAW photos)?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether uploads can go through the app server directly or need a pre-signed direct-to-storage upload URL to avoid app servers being tied up moving large files.

#### Q: Should identical images uploaded by different users be stored once or once per user?
*Why it matters:* Deduplicating identical bytes (via a content hash) can meaningfully cut storage costs at scale, but it also means one physical blob can now be referenced by many logical images, which has real implications for deletion (you can't just delete the blob when one user removes their copy).

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can upload an image and receive a shareable URL.
- The system generates and stores a small set of standard resolutions per image (e.g. thumbnail, medium, original).
- Anyone with the link can view/download an image at a given resolution.
- A user can delete an image they uploaded.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Image reads must be fast and low-latency globally, since viewing images is the overwhelming majority of all traffic.**
- **The system must be durable: an uploaded image must not be lost, ever, once the upload is acknowledged as successful.**
- **The system must scale to storing billions of images and serving very high read volume without every read hitting origin storage.**
- **Uploads should not block on resizing; the original should be available (or an upload acknowledged) even while thumbnails are still being generated.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 million images uploaded per day
- Average original image size is 3 MB; 3 derived resolutions are generated per image, averaging 500 KB combined
- Read-to-write ratio of roughly 50:1 (images are viewed far more than uploaded)
- Images are retained indefinitely (no automatic expiry)

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Upload QPS:** 10,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 116 uploads/sec average, design for 5-10x at peak ≈ 1,000/sec
- **Read QPS:** 50:1 ratio on 10M uploads/day ≈ 500 million reads/day ≈ 5,800 reads/sec average, tens of thousands/sec at peak
- **Storage growth per day:** 10,000,000 * (3 MB original + 0.5 MB derived) ≈ 35 TB/day, which is roughly 12.7 PB/year, far beyond what any single disk or machine can hold
- **5-year storage footprint:** 12.7 PB/year * 5 ≈ 63.5 PB, confirming this must be built on a horizontally scaled object store (like S3), never a traditional filesystem on a fixed set of servers

*Capacity Takeaway:* This system is dominated by two facts at once: storage grows into the **tens of petabytes** within a few years (ruling out anything but object storage), and reads outnumber writes **50 to 1** (ruling out serving directly from that object store without a CDN in front of it), so the architecture is really 'object store plus CDN' with everything else in service of those two decisions.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A client uploads an image; the app server computes a content hash, checks
blob_refcounts to see if identical bytes already exist (dedup), stores the
metadata row, writes the original to object storage if it's new, and
enqueues a resizing job rather than generating derived resolutions inline.
A pool of resize workers pulls from that queue, generates the standard
resolutions, writes each to object storage, and records a row per variant.
Reads never hit the app server or origin storage in the common case: a CDN
sits in front of the object store, caching each resolution's bytes at edge
locations close to the requester, so the overwhelming majority of the
50-to-1 read traffic is served from the edge.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Upload (write) path and view (read) path

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    metadb[("Metadata DB")]:::db
    queue>"Resize Queue"]:::queue
    worker["Resize Workers"]:::server
    blobstore["Object Storage"]:::server
    cdn["CDN"]:::server
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"write metadata"| metadb
    app -->|"store original"| blobstore
    app -.->|"enqueue resize"| queue
    queue -.-> worker
    worker -.->|"write variants"| blobstore
    cdn -->|"origin pull on miss"| blobstore
    client -->|"view image"| cdn
```

#### An upload, from click to viewable

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Client uploads image (POST /api/images)"]:::step
    step_2["2. App server hashes bytes (check for existing blob)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Original stored, metadata written (upload acknowledged to user)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Resize job enqueued (async, does not block response)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Worker generates variants (thumbnail, medium, etc.)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Variants pushed to CDN edge on first view (origin pull and cache)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### When to generate resized variants

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  upload["Image uploaded"] --> mode{"When to generate sizes?"}
  mode -->|"eager"| sync["Generate all sizes before response"]
  mode -->|"lazy"| onreq["Generate on first request"]
  mode -->|"async queue"| queue["Return fast, worker generates later"]
  sync --> slow["Upload latency goes up"]
  onreq --> firstpen["First viewer pays the penalty"]
  queue --> best["Fast upload, ready before most views"]
```

#### Cumulative storage growth over 5 years

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/images` | Body: multipart image data (or a request for a pre-signed direct-upload URL for large files). Returns an image_id and status (processing/ready). |
| `GET` | `/api/images/{imageId}` | Query param ?size=thumbnail|medium|original. Redirects to (or streams from) the CDN-backed URL for that resolution. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/images/{imageId}` | Deletes an image and its derived resolutions, owner-authenticated. |
| `GET` | `/api/images/{imageId}/status` | Returns processing status, useful for a client polling to know when all derived resolutions are ready after upload. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `images`
- `image_id (unique, indexed)`
- `owner_id (indexed)`
- `content_hash (hash of original bytes, indexed, used for deduplication)`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
- `status (uploading | processing | ready | deleted)`
*Notes:* The metadata source of truth. content_hash is the key that makes deduplication possible: two uploads with the same hash point at the same underlying blob.

### Entity: `image_variants`
- `image_id (indexed)`
- `resolution (thumbnail | medium | original)`
- `storage_key (the blob's path/key in object storage)`
- `width, height, byte_size`
*Notes:* One row per generated resolution per image. Kept separate from images so a variant can be regenerated or backfilled without touching the parent record.

### Entity: `blob_refcounts`
- `content_hash (primary key)`
- `reference_count (integer)`
*Notes:* Tracks how many logical images point at a deduplicated physical blob, so deleting one user's image only deletes the underlying bytes when the reference count hits zero.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Where and when do you generate the derived resolutions (thumbnail, medium)?
Two real approaches exist. Eager: generate all standard resolutions synchronously during upload, so by the time the upload response comes back, everything is ready to serve. Lazy: store only the original at upload time, and generate a given resolution on first request, caching the result after. Most production systems use a queue-based hybrid: upload returns immediately once the original is durably stored, and a worker pool generates the standard resolutions asynchronously in the background, typically finishing within seconds.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Eager (synchronous) generation: the upload response guarantees every resolution is ready, but uploads become slow and resizing work competes directly with app server capacity for user-facing request latency
- Lazy (on first request) generation: uploads are instant, and resolutions nobody ever requests are never generated, but the first viewer of any given resolution pays a noticeable latency penalty
- Async queue-based generation (used in practice): uploads return fast, resizing work is isolated on a dedicated worker fleet that can scale independently of the app servers, and nearly all resolutions are ready well before most viewers arrive, at the cost of a brief 'still processing' window right after upload

### How do you deduplicate identical images without breaking per-user deletion?
Hashing the original bytes (e.g. SHA-256) on upload lets the system detect that a new upload is byte-identical to an existing blob and skip storing it again, just adding a new images metadata row that points at the same storage_key. The catch is that a blob can now be shared by many logical images, so a naive 'delete removes the blob' would corrupt other users' images. The fix is a reference count per content_hash: deleting an image decrements the count and only deletes the physical blob when it reaches zero.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- No deduplication: simplest to reason about (one image, one blob, one owner), but storage cost scales with total uploads even when the same viral image is re-uploaded by thousands of users
- Content-hash deduplication with reference counting: meaningfully cuts storage for popular re-uploaded content, but adds a hash lookup on every upload and requires the reference-count bookkeeping to be correct under concurrent deletes, or you risk either leaking storage or deleting a blob still in use

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Object storage itself (e.g. S3-style) is already horizontally scaled by the provider, so the real bottleneck shifts to the metadata database; shard it by image_id or owner_id once it exceeds what a single instance can serve.
- The resize worker fleet must scale independently of app servers, since resizing is CPU-bound and bursty (a single popular account's bulk upload shouldn't starve normal traffic); this is exactly what a queue in front of the workers is for.
- The CDN's cache hit rate is the single biggest lever on cost and latency; a long TTL is safe here because, like the URL shortener, an image's bytes at a given resolution never change once generated, so there is no cache-invalidation problem to solve.
- The blob_refcounts table becomes a hotspot for extremely popular deduplicated images (many uploads and deletes referencing the same hash); an atomic increment/decrement operation (not read-modify-write) is required to avoid races at scale.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Generating all resolutions synchronously== during the upload request, making uploads slow and coupling resize CPU load directly to app server request latency.
- ⚠️ Storing images directly in a relational database as large binary blobs instead of using object storage designed for this, which does not scale past a fairly small dataset size.
- ⚠️ Deduplicating by exact filename or file size instead of a **content hash**, which either misses true duplicates or falsely merges different images.
- ⚠️ ==Deleting the underlying blob== the moment one user deletes their image, without checking whether other users' images (via deduplication) still reference the same bytes.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why put a CDN in front of the object store instead of just making the object store fast enough?**

> **Model Answer:** Because latency is dominated by physical distance for a globally distributed user base; even a very fast origin store in one region is slow for a user on another continent. A CDN caches bytes at edge locations near the requester, and since image bytes are immutable once generated, there is no invalidation cost to caching them aggressively and for a long time.

**Q: What happens if two users upload the exact same image at the same moment, before deduplication has recorded either one?**

> **Model Answer:** This is a race condition on the content_hash check-then-write. It's handled the same way as any uniqueness race: attempt an atomic insert or increment on blob_refcounts keyed by content_hash, and whichever request loses the race simply reuses the winner's storage_key instead of writing a second copy, rather than trying to check-then-act non-atomically in the application layer.

# Design an Image Hosting Service (like Flickr)

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Flickr • Imgur` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> An image is immutable binary data with structured metadata bolted on, so the entire design comes down to separating those two concerns cleanly: a **blob store** built for cheap, massive, mostly-write-once binary storage, and a small database that only tracks where each blob lives and what it's called.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design an image hosting service: a user uploads an image, the system stores
it and generates a few common resolutions (thumbnail, medium, full-size),
and anyone with the link can view the image quickly from anywhere in the
world. Design the system end to end. You don't need to design a full social
network around it, just the upload, storage, resizing, and serving.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the read-to-write ratio, and how much does traffic concentrate on a small number of popular images?
*Why it matters:* Image hosting is typically extremely read-heavy, and popularity is skewed (a handful of images get most of the views). That skew is what justifies putting a CDN in front of nearly everything rather than serving directly from storage.

#### Q: Do we need to generate multiple resolutions (thumbnail, medium, full-size), or serve the exact bytes that were uploaded?
*Why it matters:* Multi-resolution support means an asynchronous processing pipeline has to exist between upload and 'the image is fully available', which changes both the write path and the data model (one logical image, several physical variants).

#### Q: What's the maximum image size and expected upload volume, and do we need to support very large original files (e.g. RAW photos)?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether uploads can go through the app server directly or need a pre-signed direct-to-storage upload URL to avoid app servers being tied up moving large files.

#### Q: Should identical images uploaded by different users be stored once or once per user?
*Why it matters:* Deduplicating identical bytes (via a content hash) can meaningfully cut storage costs at scale, but it also means one physical blob can now be referenced by many logical images, which has real implications for deletion (you can't just delete the blob when one user removes their copy).

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can upload an image and receive a shareable URL.
- The system generates and stores a small set of standard resolutions per image (e.g. thumbnail, medium, original).
- Anyone with the link can view/download an image at a given resolution.
- A user can delete an image they uploaded.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Image reads must be fast and low-latency globally, since viewing images is the overwhelming majority of all traffic.**
- **The system must be durable: an uploaded image must not be lost, ever, once the upload is acknowledged as successful.**
- **The system must scale to storing billions of images and serving very high read volume without every read hitting origin storage.**
- **Uploads should not block on resizing; the original should be available (or an upload acknowledged) even while thumbnails are still being generated.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 million images uploaded per day
- Average original image size is 3 MB; 3 derived resolutions are generated per image, averaging 500 KB combined
- Read-to-write ratio of roughly 50:1 (images are viewed far more than uploaded)
- Images are retained indefinitely (no automatic expiry)

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Upload QPS:** 10,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 116 uploads/sec average, design for 5-10x at peak ≈ 1,000/sec
- **Read QPS:** 50:1 ratio on 10M uploads/day ≈ 500 million reads/day ≈ 5,800 reads/sec average, tens of thousands/sec at peak
- **Storage growth per day:** 10,000,000 * (3 MB original + 0.5 MB derived) ≈ 35 TB/day, which is roughly 12.7 PB/year, far beyond what any single disk or machine can hold
- **5-year storage footprint:** 12.7 PB/year * 5 ≈ 63.5 PB, confirming this must be built on a horizontally scaled object store (like S3), never a traditional filesystem on a fixed set of servers

*Capacity Takeaway:* This system is dominated by two facts at once: storage grows into the **tens of petabytes** within a few years (ruling out anything but object storage), and reads outnumber writes **50 to 1** (ruling out serving directly from that object store without a CDN in front of it), so the architecture is really 'object store plus CDN' with everything else in service of those two decisions.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A client uploads an image; the app server computes a content hash, checks
blob_refcounts to see if identical bytes already exist (dedup), stores the
metadata row, writes the original to object storage if it's new, and
enqueues a resizing job rather than generating derived resolutions inline.
A pool of resize workers pulls from that queue, generates the standard
resolutions, writes each to object storage, and records a row per variant.
Reads never hit the app server or origin storage in the common case: a CDN
sits in front of the object store, caching each resolution's bytes at edge
locations close to the requester, so the overwhelming majority of the
50-to-1 read traffic is served from the edge.

```

#### Cumulative storage growth over 5 years

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/images` | Body: multipart image data (or a request for a pre-signed direct-upload URL for large files). Returns an image_id and status (processing/ready). |
| `GET` | `/api/images/{imageId}` | Query param ?size=thumbnail|medium|original. Redirects to (or streams from) the CDN-backed URL for that resolution. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/images/{imageId}` | Deletes an image and its derived resolutions, owner-authenticated. |
| `GET` | `/api/images/{imageId}/status` | Returns processing status, useful for a client polling to know when all derived resolutions are ready after upload. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `images`
- `image_id (unique, indexed)`
- `owner_id (indexed)`
- `content_hash (hash of original bytes, indexed, used for deduplication)`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
- `status (uploading | processing | ready | deleted)`
*Notes:* The metadata source of truth. content_hash is the key that makes deduplication possible: two uploads with the same hash point at the same underlying blob.

### Entity: `image_variants`
- `image_id (indexed)`
- `resolution (thumbnail | medium | original)`
- `storage_key (the blob's path/key in object storage)`
- `width, height, byte_size`
*Notes:* One row per generated resolution per image. Kept separate from images so a variant can be regenerated or backfilled without touching the parent record.

### Entity: `blob_refcounts`
- `content_hash (primary key)`
- `reference_count (integer)`
*Notes:* Tracks how many logical images point at a deduplicated physical blob, so deleting one user's image only deletes the underlying bytes when the reference count hits zero.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Where and when do you generate the derived resolutions (thumbnail, medium)?
Two real approaches exist. Eager: generate all standard resolutions synchronously during upload, so by the time the upload response comes back, everything is ready to serve. Lazy: store only the original at upload time, and generate a given resolution on first request, caching the result after. Most production systems use a queue-based hybrid: upload returns immediately once the original is durably stored, and a worker pool generates the standard resolutions asynchronously in the background, typically finishing within seconds.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Eager (synchronous) generation: the upload response guarantees every resolution is ready, but uploads become slow and resizing work competes directly with app server capacity for user-facing request latency
- Lazy (on first request) generation: uploads are instant, and resolutions nobody ever requests are never generated, but the first viewer of any given resolution pays a noticeable latency penalty
- Async queue-based generation (used in practice): uploads return fast, resizing work is isolated on a dedicated worker fleet that can scale independently of the app servers, and nearly all resolutions are ready well before most viewers arrive, at the cost of a brief 'still processing' window right after upload

### How do you deduplicate identical images without breaking per-user deletion?
Hashing the original bytes (e.g. SHA-256) on upload lets the system detect that a new upload is byte-identical to an existing blob and skip storing it again, just adding a new images metadata row that points at the same storage_key. The catch is that a blob can now be shared by many logical images, so a naive 'delete removes the blob' would corrupt other users' images. The fix is a reference count per content_hash: deleting an image decrements the count and only deletes the physical blob when it reaches zero.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- No deduplication: simplest to reason about (one image, one blob, one owner), but storage cost scales with total uploads even when the same viral image is re-uploaded by thousands of users
- Content-hash deduplication with reference counting: meaningfully cuts storage for popular re-uploaded content, but adds a hash lookup on every upload and requires the reference-count bookkeeping to be correct under concurrent deletes, or you risk either leaking storage or deleting a blob still in use

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- Object storage itself (e.g. S3-style) is already horizontally scaled by the provider, so the real bottleneck shifts to the metadata database; shard it by image_id or owner_id once it exceeds what a single instance can serve.
- The resize worker fleet must scale independently of app servers, since resizing is CPU-bound and bursty (a single popular account's bulk upload shouldn't starve normal traffic); this is exactly what a queue in front of the workers is for.
- The CDN's cache hit rate is the single biggest lever on cost and latency; a long TTL is safe here because, like the URL shortener, an image's bytes at a given resolution never change once generated, so there is no cache-invalidation problem to solve.
- The blob_refcounts table becomes a hotspot for extremely popular deduplicated images (many uploads and deletes referencing the same hash); an atomic increment/decrement operation (not read-modify-write) is required to avoid races at scale.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Generating all resolutions synchronously== during the upload request, making uploads slow and coupling resize CPU load directly to app server request latency.
- ⚠️ Storing images directly in a relational database as large binary blobs instead of using object storage designed for this, which does not scale past a fairly small dataset size.
- ⚠️ Deduplicating by exact filename or file size instead of a **content hash**, which either misses true duplicates or falsely merges different images.
- ⚠️ ==Deleting the underlying blob== the moment one user deletes their image, without checking whether other users' images (via deduplication) still reference the same bytes.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why put a CDN in front of the object store instead of just making the object store fast enough?**

> **Model Answer:** Because latency is dominated by physical distance for a globally distributed user base; even a very fast origin store in one region is slow for a user on another continent. A CDN caches bytes at edge locations near the requester, and since image bytes are immutable once generated, there is no invalidation cost to caching them aggressively and for a long time.

**Q: What happens if two users upload the exact same image at the same moment, before deduplication has recorded either one?**

> **Model Answer:** This is a race condition on the content_hash check-then-write. It's handled the same way as any uniqueness race: attempt an atomic insert or increment on blob_refcounts keyed by content_hash, and whichever request loses the race simply reuses the winner's storage_key instead of writing a second copy, rather than trying to check-then-act non-atomically in the application layer.
